context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. All right, good.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President——

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Critical Minerals Supply

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Would that include security guarantees for Ukraine?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. What?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Would a minerals deal include a security guarantee for Ukraine?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, it will be—Europe is going to make sure that nothing happens. I don't think it's going to be much of a problem. I think once we settle, there's going to be no more war in Ukraine, and you're not going to have it. It's not going to be a very big problem. That's going to be the least of it.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Greece

context.text: Q. Mr. President, we're hearing from the Greek——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Are you going to meet with President Zelensky soon?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. ——media reporting that the U.S. has agreed to shut down a military base in Greece that's been a logistical hub for NATO.

context.speaker: Trump

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. That the U.S. has agreed to shut it down at the request of Turkey and Russia. Is that at all true?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Marco, do you have anything to say——

context.speaker: Secretary of Defense Peter B. Hegseth
context.text: Secretary of Defense Peter B. Hegseth. No.
context.source_speaker_label: Secretary of Defense Peter B. Hegseth

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Russia

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, how do you react to people in Europe who say that you are abandoning Ukraine and that you are going to sacrifice the security of Ukraine by making a deal with Vladimir Putin?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. No, we're helping Ukraine like nobody has ever helped Ukraine before.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I can say this: If I didn't become President, Ukraine would, right now, still be at a level where there would be no even thinking about a peace. And it was a—it's a sad thing that this happened. This would have never happened, this war, if I were President. Zero chance.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And it has happened, so my function is to get you out of the war, get them out of the war.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Let them live. It's a bloody war. It's a horrible war.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Thousands of people are being killed a week. And I would say, Russia—maybe 700,000 people. I think Ukraine, probably, a similar number. And that's not talking about the towns and the cities that have been blown up. That's talking about soldiers. This has been a horrible bloody mess, and we're going to get it solved. We've got to get it solved.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And you know, we're not talking about America's soldiers—soldiers from this country.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We're talking about Russia and Ukraine. But on a humanitarian basis, we have to get this very, very bloody, savage problem solved.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I will say this also, it could lead to World War III if it's not solved. You know, there'll be a point at which it's not going to stop at those two countries. Already, there's such involvement from other countries, and it could really lead to a very big war—World War III. And we're not going to let that happen either.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/European Military Assistance

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Will you support the idea to send European troops in Ukraine to back the cease-fire?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes, European troops may go into Ukraine as peacemakers, so when the agreement is done, they can watch that everything is followed properly. I don't think that's going to be a problem. And a lot of the European countries, I think—I don't want to speak for France, but I know that the President has talked about doing that also.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I think that will be a very good day when we can go in as peacekeepers, as opposed to what's going on right now with everybody being killed. So——

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: European Military Assistance/Ukraine

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Will they have U.S. backing? Those troops going into Ukraine, will they have U.S. backing from U.S. troops?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, we're going to have a backing of some kind, and obviously the European countries are going to be involved. And I don't think you're going to need much backing. I think that's not going to be a problem.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Once an agreement is signed, Russia is going to get back to its business, and Ukraine and Europe are going to get back to their business. I don't think it's going to be a problem.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, could——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Can you talk about DOGE?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. ——you meet with President Zelenskyy soon?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. What?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Could you meet with President Zelenskyy soon? With the——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I will be meeting with President Zelenskyy. In fact, he may come in this week or next week to sign the agreement and—which would be nice, I'd love to meet him. We'd meet at the Oval Office.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So the agreement is being worked on now. They're very close to a final deal. It will be a deal with rare earths and various other things. And he would like to come, as I understand it, here, to sign it, and that would be great with me.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I think they then have to get it approved by their council or whoever might approve it. But I'm sure that will happen.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [At this point, several reporters began asking questions at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: President Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin of Russia

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. How soon, Mr. President, are you planning to meet with President Putin?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President Macron——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. At some point, I'll be meeting with President Putin also, yes.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. How soon?

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I don't know when. We speak. We're trying to get this thing worked out.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But yes, at some point I'll be meeting with President Putin too.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once. A reporter then spoke in French; no translation was provided.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Say it.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. I can say a few words in French.

context.speaker: Mixed
context.text: President Trump. Yes, please. [President Macron spoke in French.] President Macron. President Trump——

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once. President Trump then addressed an interpreter as follows.] President Trump. Yes.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [An interpreter translated President Macron's remarks as follows.]

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. ——has already spoken about this just a moment ago. This is exactly what we want to do. We want to build peace with Ukraine. As President Trump mentioned, there are already 1 million dead and wounded in Ukraine since the war began. We had a cease-fire in the past that was not respected. This was under the Minsk agreements I and II.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Trump, as he said, will be meeting with President Zelenskyy to sign a deal on rare earths, and we are pleased to see this very strong American involvement.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: Europe, of course, also stands ready to support Ukraine in various ways, supporting its military. And we don't want to preempt any sort of discussions that are currently underway, but we do share the same objective of building this lasting peace.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I just want to tell you a little story. So we were at the Eiffel Tower having dinner with your wonderful wife and with my wonderful wife, and we came out, and he started speaking the French deal, and we didn't have an interpreter. And he was going on and on and on, and I was just nodding, "Yes, yes, yes." [Laughter] And he really sold me out, because I got back the next day, and I read the papers. I said, "That's not what we said." [Laughter]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: He's a smart customer, I will tell you that. Do you remember? That was—— [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: ——that was—that wasn't exactly what we agreed to.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine/Russian Conflict

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, you called Zelenskyy a dictator. Would you use the same words regarding Putin?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I don't use those words lightly. I think that we're going to see how it all works out. Let's see what happens.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I think we have a chance of a really good settlement between various countries. And, you know, you're talking about Europe, and you're talking about Ukraine as part of that whole situation. The other side has a lot of support also. So let's see how it all works out. It might work out.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Look, you can never make up lives. They're the one thing you can't. You can make up the money, but you can't make up the lives. A lot of lives lost. I think probably a lot more lives than people are talking about. That's been a—it's been a rough war, but I think we're close to getting it solved.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Go ahead.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Russia/Critical Minerals Supply

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Can you clarify what you meant in your Truth today on the major economic development transactions between the U.S. and Russia? Any more details there?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. With respect to what? Russia?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. In solving a peace deal. You said there would be "major economic development transactions which will take place between the United States and Russia."

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes. We're trying to do some economic development deals. They have a lot of things that we want, and we'll see. I mean, I don't know if that will come to fruition, but we'd love to be able to do that, if we could.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You know, they have massive rare earth. It's a very large—it's actually the largest. In terms of land, it's by far the largest country. And they have very valuable things that we could use, and we have things that they could use, and it would be very good. If we could do that, I think it would be a very good thing for world peace and lasting peace.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: It will—I mean, our first—by far, our first thing that we want to do or the first element of— of the overall transaction is ending the war. But if—just as we're doing with Ukraine, if we could do some economic development in terms of Russia and getting things that we want, something like that would be possible, yes.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President—Mr. President—— [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Can you explain the rationale, sir, in the U.S. voting——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes. Go ahead, please.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Can you explain the rationale in having the U.S. vote against the U.N. resolutions that Ukraine proposed and also the U.S. proposed?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I would rather not explain it now, but it's sort of self-evident, I think.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Russia

context.speaker: Mixed
context.text: Q. When do you think the war would end, Mr. President? [A reporter spoke in French; no translation was provided.] President Trump. I think the war could end soon.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. How soon?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Within weeks.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Weeks?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes, I think so.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. At what price for Ukraine.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Right? Don't you think so? I'd like to ask—have you—I think we could end it within weeks if we're smart. If we're not smart, it will keep going, and we'll keep losing young, beautiful people that shouldn't be dying, and we don't want that.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. What is the price for Ukraine?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. And remember what I said: This could escalate into a third world war, and we don't want that either.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Russia/Ukraine

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, your Envoy, Steve Witkoff, suggested a temporary cease-fire in the conflict, but the Russian Government has denied that out of hand. Are you worried that they're not dealing in good faith?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. No, I think they, at some point, will agree to that. I think they probably want it too. And I think, once you have a cease-fire, it's going to end because they're not going from a cease-fire back to war. I think people have had their full.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I'm just glad I was able to help, because there was no communication with Russia until I came along. Biden didn't communicate. He couldn't communicate with his own child. So Biden didn't communicate. He couldn't—he—it was terrible. He hadn't spoken to Putin in 3 years.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You're trying to end a war. People are being killed. Every week, thousands of people are being killed—soldiers, in this case, mostly. Also, towns, you know, as missiles go in and back and forth.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: No, it's a shame. This should have never happened. This is a very sad—this is going to go down in the history books. This a very sad moment, because that should have been stopped. That should have never started. And if it did start, it should have stopped the first week, not 3 years later. Okay?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. What do you think would be the price for Ukraine?

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. [Inaudible]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Please.

context.speaker: Mixed
context.text: President Macron. If you'll allow me, because I had just—— [President Macron spoke in French; no translation was provided.] President Trump. By the way, that is the most——
source_speaker_runs: President Macron spoke in French; no translation was provided

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. That is the most beautiful language. [Laughter] I have no idea what he's saying, but that is the most——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: [President Macron spoke in English as follows.] President Macron. She will translate.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. ——elegant, beautiful language. Go ahead, please.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: It's true. It's very——

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [An interpreter translated President Macron's remarks as follows.]

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. This is a question that was asked by several. What we need to do is make sure that we are building peace. We have deterrence——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Can you speak up, please?

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [The interpreter continued her translation as follows.]

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. We have deterrence capabilities that have been restored. As President Trump said, there won't be any more problems. We've seen the U.S. reengagement and the message that that sends to Mr. Putin. We have deterrence, which will allow a truce to take place. Verification of that truce and then a peace agreement can be put in place so that we can start rebuilding Ukraine with security guarantees. And we have a role to play in that.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: Again, I'm not preempting any discussions, but we've spoken about Ukraine sovereignty, and that has been a subject of discussion between the U.S. and Ukraine.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: We have also been working closely with our British partners this week. We've shared this information with other European countries, and we are ready and willing to provide those security

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: guarantees, which could perhaps include troops, but they would be there to maintain peace. They would not be along the front lines. They would not be part of any conflict. They would be there to ensure that the peace is respected.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: Our assistance may include other capacity-building, perhaps, for the military. We see U.S. credibility here. We each have our role to play, but it will be done in a united fashion.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Group of Seven (G–7) Nations

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, do you think that Ukraine should give up on part of its territory?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, we're going to see. It's a negotiation that's just starting, and, you know, they've been fighting, and there's been a lot of land that's been taken. So we'll have to see how that works out. That's part of the negotiation.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I will say there was great unity in that room today. You know, we were via Skype or whatever. But it was great—tremendous unity today in that room with the other countries. I was—

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Ukraine wants their territory——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Is France going to——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I was very impressed by it.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. ——territories back. Can they take it back, what they lost in the past years?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. That's not an easy thing to do, is it? Right? It's not an easy—you know, he's asking whether or not you can take back the land that they lost. And I say that, yes, perhaps some of it, yes. I hope so. But that's not an easy thing to do.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. But not everything?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. For Macron, on the frozen Russian——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. It's going to be something we're talking about.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, on the frozen——

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: President Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin of Russia

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Will you convince Vladimir Putin to accept the European troops as peacekeeper? What do you think——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes, he will accept that.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. He will accept them?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I've asked him that question.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. You talked to him about it?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I've asked him that question.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. He said yes?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Is France going to lift the block on the $300 billion——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Because he's not—look, if we do this deal, he's not looking for more war.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: He doesn't mind.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But I've specifically asked him that question. He has no problem with it.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Is France going to lift the block on the $300 billion in frozen Russian assets in Belgium? France has opposed unfreezing it to pay Ukraine and compensate the U.S. for its support. Is France going to lift its opposition to that?

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. This is frozen—I mean, we speak about frozen assets? We already used them to backs precisely the loans negotiated at the G–7. And it's part of the sanctions, so it will depend on the follow-up of the discussions.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: But clearly, we respect international law. It's just frozen assets now. You can take the proceeds of the frozen assets, but you cannot take the assets themselves, because it's not respecting international law, and we want to respect international law.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. How is one different than the other? If you can take the proceeds from it, how can you not take the assets?

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. Because it's very different. You keep the assets. You take the proceeds, because they are paralyzed in a certain way. You take the proceeds during the war time, but you keep the assets, and it's part of the negotiation at the end of the war. Because, I mean, this war costed all of us a lot of money, and this is the responsibility of Russia, because the aggressor is Russia. So——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Should the U.S. be compensated?

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. So, at the end of the day, this frozen asset should be part of the negotiation, all in all.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/International Security Assistance

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Will France support the U.S. being compensated?

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. I support the idea to have Ukraine first being compensated, because they are the one to have lose a lot of their fellow citizens and are being destroyed by these attacks.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: Second, all of those who paid for could be compensated, but not by Ukraine, by Russia, because they were the one to aggress.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Again, just so you understand. [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Just so you understand, Europe is loaning the money to Ukraine. They get their money back. President Macron. No, in fact, to be frank, we paid—we paid 60 percent of the total defaults. President Trump. Okay.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. And it was through, like the U.S., loans, guarantee, grants, and we provided real money, to be clear.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes, okay.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. We have $230 billion frozen assets in Europe—Russian assets—but this is not as a collateral of a loan, because this is not our belonging. So they are frozen.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: If, at the end of the day in the negotiation, we will have with Russia, they're ready to give— to give it to us, super. It will be loan at the end of the day, and Russia will have paid for that. This is my wish.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. If you believe that, it's okay with me.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, do you——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. But they get their money back. We don't, and now we do. But you know, that's only fair.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. Well, we fight—[inaudible]. [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Russia/Ukraine

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, do you think Russia should be the one that pays everybody back? Are they the aggressors?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, we're all—we're negotiating everything, and everything is on the table. And we'll see if we can get some land back, and we'll see about a lot of different things.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And we're going to be making a little speech and say a few words in a little while. We're going to have another meeting, a luncheon meeting. And we'll see you in about 2 hours. Okay?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Thank you very much, everybody.

context.speaker: President Macron
context.text: President Macron. Thank you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Thank you. Thank you very much.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I also want to thank Emmanuel for hosting me in Paris last December after a historic election win to witness the reopening of the spectacular Notre Dame Cathedral, where you did an outstanding job in bringing it back together. That was a sad day, watching that burn. And 5 years later, you had it up, and it was, they say, more beautiful than it was before. So I think that's a great achievement. That was not easy.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: France is America's oldest ally. Our cherished partnership has been a force for freedom, prosperity, and peace from the very beginning. We're now working on some very interesting developments—one, in particular, as you know, the war between Russia and Ukraine.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: In the American Revolution, French support helped us to seize our destiny as an independent nation. In the first and second World Wars, our citizens shed blood together on the battlefields of Europe. And I'll never forget joining President Macron 6 years ago on the 75th anniversary of D- Day. That was some day.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The purpose of our meeting today is to end another battle, a really horrible one—a war, something that we haven't seen since the Second World War—that is ravaging European soil. The deadliest and most destructive conflict that one can imagine. I've seen the pictures. I've seen the satellite photos and—and lots of other photos, and it's a horrible thing that's happening.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Thousands of people are dying a week.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: This very day is the third anniversary of the invasion of Ukraine, which would never have happened if I was President. That was not going to happen. The horrors of this gruesome and bloody war can scarcely be overestimated. Hundreds of thousands of people—Russians and Ukrainians, in particular—have needlessly died. An entire generation of Ukrainians and Russian men has been decimated. One-thousand-year-old cities have been turned into rubble. Those beautiful spires that you used to see there—they were the most beautiful in the world, they say— are lying in heaps of rubble, blasted to smithereens.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And it's time to end this bloodletting and restore peace, and I think we're going to do it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We've had some great conversations, including with Russia. Since my return to the White House, we've made more progress toward that goal in 1 month than occurred in the past 3 years.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I've spoken with both President Putin and President Zelenskyy. And, again, a lot of—a lot of good things toward peace are happening, moving it, I think, pretty quickly.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Last week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, National Security Adviser Michael Waltz, and Special Envoy Steve Witkoff conducted successful talks in Saudi Arabia with the delegation from Russia, and I'd like to thank the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia and the King and Muhammad. context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Our focus is on achieving a cease-fire as soon as possible and ultimately a permanent peace. My meeting with President Macron today was another important step forward in that—well, that sphere, because he's been very much involved, right from the beginning, on trying to get it over with, and we're going to get it done.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I believe that Emmanuel agrees with me on many of the most important issues. Chief among them is, this is the right time. It may be the only time.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You know, that's a very interesting and horrible situation, and that could evolve into a third world war. We're not going to let that happen. It should have never started, but it did, and what a mess. What a horrible, bloody mess.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I'm also pleased that President Macron agrees that the cost and burden of securing the peace must be borne by the nations of Europe, not alone by the United States. And Europe must take that central role in assuring long-term security of Ukraine, which they want to do. And that's not a very big step. A big step is what's going to happen over the next few weeks.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The United States has put up far more aid for Ukraine than any other nation, hundreds of billions of dollars. We have other things happening that maybe take that out of the realm of necessity.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And while we've given vast amounts of military aid and money in form of grants, much of Europe's contribution has been economic relief structured as loans, for which they'll be repaid. Like the Europeans, I believe that taxpayers and the United States also deserve to recoup the colossal amounts of money that we've sent. The previous administration never even thought of that. They didn't think of a lot of things, like why did they let it start in the first place.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: That is why we must have an agreement with Ukraine on critical minerals and rare earths and various other things as security. And I think that that's happening. I think we've made a lot of progress. I had a report just given to me before walking in that we've made, Emmanuel, a great deal of progress toward getting that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I've been elected by the American people to restore common sense to Washington and, indeed, to the world. And I believe strongly that it's in the best interest of the United States, the best interest in Europe, the best interest of Ukraine, and indeed, the best interest of Russia to stop the killing now and bring the world to peace.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: My administration is making a decisive break with the foreign policy failures of the past administration and, frankly, the past. I ran against a very foolish foreign policy establishment, and their recklessness has led to the death of many, many people.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Under our administration, we're forging a new path that promotes peace around the world.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And when I left office for the first administration—first term, we had no wars. We had no problems. We didn't have October 7 with Israel. We didn't have Russia and Ukraine going at it. context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And you know what else we didn't have? Millions of people pouring through our borders, many of them criminals released from other nations and put right into our land: murderers and drug dealers, gangs. We didn't have any of that. It's a different time.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But now we have it, and we're fixing it. We'll fix it all up. We'll get it done as quickly as possible.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: Mr. President, I really wish to thank you for making changes to your schedule to meet with us so quickly. I think we've made very substantive steps forward during our discussions, and this is a major step in what we're experiencing today.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: We had a video conference with all of the G–7 leaders, which was an opportunity for us to discuss this matter 3 days [years; White House correction] after the Russian war in Ukraine, and to express our support for President Zelenskyy, to the Ukrainian people, but also to speak and share about our desire for a lasting peace. This is what we have spoken about very forcibly over the past few weeks.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: We thought that this war was only going to last a few weeks when it broke out in 2022. We admire greatly the courage of the Ukrainian people.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: And, Mr. President, I wish to thank you for this. Ukraine has been able to hold the front of our collective security. context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: Over the past few hours—and as you mentioned this, Mr. President—we've been able to see a few things take shape. And I think that's very commendable.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: We also have a shared desire to build peace. We will have this responsibility. This is 10 years after the war started in Crimea, and then we saw the events in Donbas—in the Donbas region and along the northern part of the country. We want to save lives. We want to bring prisoners back and bring back families and children because there is also humanitarian tragedy affecting the Ukrainian people.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: We had lengthy discussions with the President, and we spoke about our desire to bring an end to conflicts; to have a truce that is measurable, verifiable, and that enables negotiation of a lasting peace, where we will discuss not only Ukraine's reconstruction, its territories, but also the security guarantees, meaning maintaining peace over the long term.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: As I said to the President, we have experienced peace accords that were only cease-fires without ensuring security guarantees, Minsk I and II. And we want to make sure this doesn't happen again. And I know that the President has expressed the desire to be a player for peace in the region.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: I've spoken with some 30 European leaders and allies in recent days. We want to bring together these—alleys—allies, rather, and share the same vision. And for us Europeans, this is an existential issue.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: We also spoke about these issues at length with the President. We've worked with President Zelenskyy and gotten to some of the details of the various phases of the negotiation, and we've also been able to speak about some of this work with our British partners to talk about deployments of peace forces on Ukrainian soil, which are part of these security guarantees. Other countries are ready to join in this effort.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: Solidarity and support from the U.S. will be crucial to this. And I thank you, Mr. President, for beginning to work with us on this issue. context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: I also wanted to be very clear, Mr. President, about Europe's commitment. We have committed to building a lasting peace. As Europeans, we have committed to being stakeholders in these security guarantees, and we are also well aware that Europeans need to do more for security in Europe, for defense in Europe, and to more fairly share the security burden that your country has been carrying for so many years.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: Mr. President, you know how much friendship I show towards you and I have towards you since your first term. Europe is very clear eyed about this. We know what we need to do as Europeans, given the threats surrounding us and the responsibilities that we must shoulder.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: We spoke about the Versailles agenda, which allowed the Europeans to take a historic step and increase their investments. Europeans are ready to do even more and to go even farther. And several leaders said that to me before I came here to meet you.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: Mr. President, dear Donald, you spoke about this peace through strength. We fully share that, because we must recognize the sacrifices made by the Ukrainian people and what we owe to them.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: The President and I also spoke about economic matters and our desire to see more prosperity in the United States and in Europe. We had discussions which will be carried on by our teams, our ministers and secretaries, to flesh out some of those ideas. But the idea is to have fair competition and no bias within competition between our industries.

context.speaker: mesdames
context.text: Now, the American and European economies are extremely intertwined—some $1.5 billion in trade—trillion, rather, in goods and services. We also have a trade deficit, and I know that we need to look not only at goods, but also digital items and goods which you export. And we want to make a sincere commitment towards fair competition, where we have smooth trade and more investments.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes.

context.speaker: Q. ——
context.text: Q. ——had you up nine-plus points. And all of your agenda that you ran on, you're accomplishing that. You got the support of the American people, including stopping the war in Ukraine. If you can comment on the latest Harvard poll, I'd appreciate that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, I was honored by it. It was a big poll, and it's usually a poll that leans on the other side of things, the other side of the world, so to speak. context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And as I said, we've become the party of common sense, and I think that's a very important element now—common sense—because what's happening in the world and even in this country, some of the things that took place, many of them are now canceled, and the rest are being canceled as we speak. But we've moved very rapidly and, I think, very effectively.

context.speaker: President Macron

context.speaker: President Macron

favorable_source_context.text: President Trump. The relationship between President Zelenskyy and President Putin is not a good one. You've noticed, right? It's not a good one. It's not a good relationship, and we're going to have to try and work something out. Sometimes that happens.

favorable_source_context.text: I get along with both. I have a very good relationship with President Putin. I think I have a very good relationship with President Zelenskyy. favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: And hopefully—you know, we need the rare earth, and we have some here, but we don't have enough. We're—our economy is very strong, and we need a lot of things that, in some cases, we don't have here.

evidence.quote: And this week, I saw the reports, and it's—I don't even want to say what they are, but thousands of people—young people—young, vibrant people died. And we want to stop that senseless—should have never happened.

evidence.speaker: Trump
evidence.quote: This will lay the groundwork for a long-term peace agreement that will return stability to Eastern Europe and, hopefully, ensure that such a terrible war will never happen on European soil or, for that matter, anywhere again. It's a horrible thing that's going on.

evidence.speaker: Trump
evidence.quote: And you know, you went 3½ years with an administration that never even really had a meeting—they didn't have a meeting on peace, and there was no prospect of peace.

evidence.quote: I think, frankly, Russia wanted to go through the whole long deal. I don't think they do anymore. I don't think they do. We had a very big impact on that whole situation.

evidence.quote: But I don't like talking about phase two until I get phase one. Phase one is, I have to make peace. And we have to get Russia to agree. We have to get Ukraine to agree. context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I'm pleased to say that the bust of one of the Prime Minister's greatest predecessors, Winston Churchill, is now back in the rightful place in the Oval Office, and we're very proud of it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Our meeting today and the various breakout sessions we had were tremendously productive. Most importantly, I provided the Prime Minister with an update on our efforts to end the bloody and horrible war in Ukraine with Russia, which would never have happened if I were President— that was not going to happen. I promise you that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: After 3 years of hellacious conflict, approximately 1 million Ukrainians and Russians have been senselessly killed. But the number, I believe, is much higher than that. Countless schools, hospitals, towns, and beautiful ancient churches have been absolutely obliterated.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: To begin the process of ending this spiral of death, I had historic back-to-back calls with President Putin—very successful calls, I might add—and President Zelenskyy, and my team also spoke with the Secretary General of NATO on numerous occasions, and we're working very hard to get that war brought to an end. I think we've made a lot of progress, and I think it's moving along pretty rapidly.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I want to thank all of the people that are here that have been working on it, and we'll let you know what's—what happens. It will either be fairly soon, or it won't be at all.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: In addition, this week, I met with President Macron of France, as you know, and held talks with members of the G–7.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Tomorrow the progress toward peace will continue when President Zelenskyy visits the White House. He'll be here tomorrow in the early part of the day, and we'll be signing a historic agreement that will make the United States a major partner in developing Ukraine's minerals and rare earths and oil and gasses. And we have a great understanding. I think it's going to be great for Ukraine.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And we're going to be at the site, and we'll be digging. We'll be dig, dig, digging. Dig, we must. A big utility in New York, Con Edison, they used to have a saying, "Dig we must." And we will be digging.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But much of the European aid to Ukraine has been sent in the form of loans, for which they expect to be paid back, and we didn't have that honor under the Biden administration. He sent money—would just send it, money after money after money—and never had any knowledge of ever seeing it back: maybe 300 to 350 billion dollars.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But under the breakthrough agreement, very unusual, which everyone said was difficult to get—but it's really very good for Ukraine and very good for us—the American taxpayers will now effectively be reimbursed for the money and hundreds of billions of dollars poured into helping Ukraine defend itself, which, by and of itself, is a very worthy thing to do.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We've paid far more than any other country, and with most of our support, it's been paid in military—the finest weapons anywhere in the world. This includes vast amounts of military hardware, ammunition, and various other things that we now have to start rebuilding our own stockpiles.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Additionally, the minerals agreement will provide the basis for a more sustainable future relationship between the United States and Ukraine and thus stimulate the long-term prosperity that will help the Ukrainians rebuild their country. It's been demolished, and the ruined infrastructure—the infrastructure, as you know, is in very bad shape.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: In just over 1 month, our administration has already achieved more progress toward peace than years in the other administration, where they did nothing toward peace. They didn't understand what was happening.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Our approach is basically common sense. As I said, so many of the things that we do are based on common sense. If you want peace, you have to talk—both sides.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: As I discussed with Prime Minister Starmer, the next step we're making is toward a very achievable cease-fire. We hope that that can happen quickly, because thousands of young people—in this case, they—we're not talking about Americans; we're talking about Ukrainians and Russians—are being killed every week. Thousands.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And it's a rough battlefield. It's a flat piece of land, and the bullet only stops when it hits somebody.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And this week, I saw the reports, and it's—I don't even want to say what they are, but thousands of people—young people—young, vibrant people died. And we want to stop that senseless—should have never happened.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: This will lay the groundwork for a long-term peace agreement that will return stability to Eastern Europe and, hopefully, ensure that such a terrible war will never happen on European soil or, for that matter, anywhere again. It's a horrible thing that's going on.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The disaster in Ukraine shows exactly why it's so important for the United Kingdom and other NATO partners to make large investments in their defense capabilities. In many cases, 4 percent or 5 percent of GDP would be appropriate. I know that they're raising it. I just read an article, a great article about the work you're doing in the U.K., as to the military. You're raising it quite a bit, which is a great thing to do for your country.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: Prime Minister Starmer. Yes.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. It's great thing to do. It's sad that we need that, but probably need that. So, congratulations on that. I know you got it through.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: And in a few weeks, we mark VE Day, the 80th anniversary of Victory in Europe. Britain and America fought side by side to make that happen, one of the greatest moments in our history.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: We stand side by side still today, and we're focused now on bringing an enduring end to the barbaric war in Ukraine. Mr. President, I welcome your deep and personal commitment to bring peace and to stop the killing. You've created a moment of tremendous opportunity to reach a historic peace deal, a deal that I think would be celebrated in Ukraine and around the world. That is the prize. But we have to get it right.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: There's a famous slogan in the United Kingdom from after the Second World War. That is that we have to "win the peace," and that's what we must do now, because it can't be peace that rewards the aggressor or that gives encouragement to regimes like Iran. We agree history must be on the side of the peacemaker, not the invader.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: So the stakes, they couldn't be higher, and we're determined to work together to deliver a good deal.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: We discussed a plan today to reach a peace that is tough and fair, that Ukraine will help shape, that is backed by strength to stop Putin coming back for more.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: And I am working closely with other European leaders on this, and I am clear that the UK is ready to put boots on the ground and planes in the air to support a deal, working together with our allies, because that is the only way that peace will last.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: Mr. President, in this new era, you are also right that Europe must step up. And let me tell you now, I see the growing threats we face, and so the U.K. is all in. This year, we'll be giving more military aid to Ukraine than ever, and just this week, I've set out how we're shouldering more of the security burden. We're already one of the biggest spenders in NATO, and now we're going much further, delivering Britain's biggest sustained increase in defense spending since the cold war.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: This isn't just talk; it's action: rebalancing the transatlantic alliance, making us all stronger and standing up for our shared values and shared security, as Britain always has.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: And, Mr. President, it's no secret we're from different political traditions, but there's a lot that we have in common. And we believe it's not taking part that counts. What counts is winning. If you don't win, you don't deliver. And we're determined to deliver for the working people of Britain and America who want and deserve to see their lives improve.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Thank you very much. And—[inaudible]—answer.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: Prime Minister Starmer. Look, we had a really good discussion, a productive discussion, a good discussion, as a result of which our teams are now going to be working together on an economic deal. Our teams are going to be working together on security in Ukraine.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: You mentioned Canada. I think you're trying to find a divide between us that doesn't exist.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: We're the closest of nations, and we've had very good discussions——

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: North Atlantic Treaty Organization

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Mr. President, do you support article 5 of the NATO treaty? And are you concerned that it might be triggered if European peacekeeping forces end up in Ukraine?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I support it. I don't think we're going to have any reason for it. I think we're going to have a very successful peace, and I think it's going to be a long-lasting peace. And I think it's going to happen, hopefully, quickly. It—if it doesn't happen quickly, it may not happen at all.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And we want it for two reasons. Number one, I want to see—on a humane basis, I want to see soldiers stop getting shot, because, largely, it's soldiers now. Towns have been obliterated. But it's largely that.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Critical Minerals Supply

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Thank you. Mr. Prime Minister, you were asking the President today about a backstop for Europe if the peacekeeping force ends up in Ukraine. Did you feel like you got a satisfying answer for yourself and for Europe?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: And, Mr. President, if you want to comment on that as well, please do.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: Prime Minister Starmer. I thought we had a very productive discussion. Obviously, as the President says, the deal has to come first. But yes, our teams are going to be talking about how we make sure that deal sticks, is lasting, and enforced. So our teams will be talking about that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Okay. Please, blue.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, some experts think it could take more than a decade to mine the precious minerals from Ukraine. How much should the U.S. expect to receive? And when do you expect to see that come to fruition?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, we're never going to know that answer but by our being in Ukraine and doing the exploration and also the digging and taking the rare earth, which we need in our country very badly. We'll be doing a substantial amount of work, probably about—at least what we have in there, and we hope to be able to do that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You never know when it comes to that. You know, you dig, and maybe things aren't there like you think they're there. But we'll be spending a lot of time there. It will be great for Ukraine. It's like a huge economic development project. So it will be good for both countries. Okay?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Please.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Russia

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Prime Minister——

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [The reporter cleared his throat.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Excuse me. Prime Minister, you've talked about putting British soldiers' boots on the ground in Ukraine in the event that President Trump succeeds with his peace deal. But can you do that without a firm assurance that America will have our back in the form of some kind of security guarantee were Putin to breach that agreement?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: And, Mr. President, tomorrow you're seeing President Zelenskyy to sign this deal on minerals and energy that could be hugely important to the United States. Will you take the opportunity to apologize to him for calling him a dictator, while praising Vladimir Putin, who is a dictator?

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: Prime Minister Starmer. Well, Robert, let me start by saying I've been really clear today and previously that I think that European countries, including the United Kingdom, need to step up in our own defense and security. We've been doing that in recent days. You saw the announcement we made on spending just the other day.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: In addition to that, I've made it clear that the United Kingdom will play its full part in ensuring that, if there's a deal—and that we hope there is a deal in Ukraine—that that is a lasting deal that sticks. And we're obviously working with other European countries on that—France and

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: NATO, in particular. But we—I've got—I think I'm hosting 18 countries on Sunday to further our discussions.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: You heard from the President this morning that, you know, as historically has always been the case, we have each other's backs.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: And today we've been talking about the deal, how that will be a lasting deal. And coming out of this, our teams will now be talking in detail about that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. And I think we're going to have a very good meeting tomorrow—11 o'clock. And I think we're going to have a very good meeting tomorrow morning. We're going to get along really well. Okay? We have a lot of respect. I have a lot of respect for him.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We've given them a lot of equipment and a lot of money, but they have fought very bravely, no matter how you figure. They have really fought. Somebody has to use that equipment, and they have been very brave in that sense.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Yes, please. Go ahead.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Russia/Hostages Held in Gaza, Palestinian Territories

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Okay. Thank you, Mr. President. A question on Ukraine. Number one is, if you're not considering the security guarantees, are you open to other forms of, for example, intelligence cooperation with Ukraine?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: And, Mr. Prime Minister, President Trump has proposed a plan for Gaza. Does this fit into the two-state solution that the U.K. held for a long time? Do you see it fit into your general Middle Eastern strategy?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Thank you so much.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes, thank you very much. We're open to many things, but before I even think about that—that's almost pleasant to think about, because that would mean that peace has been arrived at. We have to arrive at that peace.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And you know, you went 3½ years with an administration that never even really had a meeting—they didn't have a meeting on peace, and there was no prospect of peace.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I think, frankly, Russia wanted to go through the whole long deal. I don't think they do anymore. I don't think they do. We had a very big impact on that whole situation.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But I don't like talking about phase two until I get phase one. Phase one is, I have to make peace. And we have to get Russia to agree. We have to get Ukraine to agree. And I think we will. I think we've come a long way. I believe we're going to get it done. I wouldn't say that if I didn't think so. And I think it will be very important, very historic, and we're going to save a lot of lives.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: Prime Minister Starmer. On the question of Gaza. The—the last few weeks of the ceasefire have been very impactful. And for me, there are two images that I remember more than any other. The first is Emily Damari, who is British, being reunited with her mother. You may remember she had her fingers missing after what she endured. That was an incredible moment. I had spent a lot of time with her mother while she was held captive, and her mother went through absolute torture.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: The other image was thousands of Palestinians marching through rubble, trying to return to their communities and their homes.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: So we have to do everything we can to ensure that the cease-fire continues so that more hostages can be returned, so that aid can be brought in that's desperately needed. And we—we need to allow Palestinians to return and to rebuild their lives, and we must all support them in doing that.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: And yes, I believe that the two-state solution is ultimately the only way for a lasting peace in the region.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. And think of that, she came home with her fingers and part of her hand blown off.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: Prime Minister Starmer. That's terrible.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes. How bad does it get? And we had others that came home in much, much worse shape than that.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: Prime Minister Starmer. Yes.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. It's a terrible situation. Please. Yes.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Thank you. Mr. President, did our Prime Minister persuade you not to put tariffs on the U.K.?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: And if I may, Prime Minister, do you think that Vladimir Putin is a man who is—will keep his word?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Thanks.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. He tried. [Laughter] He was working hard, I'll tell you that. [Laughter] He earned whatever the hell they pay him over there. [Laughter] But he tried.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Okay? Thank you.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Starmer
context.text: Prime Minister Starmer. On the second part of the question, I think my views on Putin are pretty well rehearsed and pretty well known. And my concern is that if there's a deal, and I hope there is a deal, that it must be a lasting deal, that it's not a temporary measure. And that is why I think it's really important that Putin knows that this deal, a historic deal, which I very much hope comes about, is there and it's a lasting deal and that we're able to deal with any inclination he has to go again or go further.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I think we'll have two deals. I think we'll have a deal on ending the war, and I think we're going to end up with a great trade deal with you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And it's an honor to be with you.

prompt_links.quote: Q. Mr. President, when and how do you envision a trilateral summit with President Zelenskyy and Putin under——

We have to negotiate a deal, but we've started the confines of a deal, and I think something can happen.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The big thing is the number of soldiers, mostly, at this point, but soldiers being killed. You're losing thousands of soldiers. On both sides, we're losing a lot of soldiers, and we want to see it stop. And we want to see the money get put to different kinds of use, like rebuilding—the rebuilding.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And we're going to be working very hard, but we've had a lot of very good conversations. I will say, until we came along, the Biden administration didn't speak to Russia whatsoever. They didn't speak to anybody. They just allowed this to continue.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I will say that—I'll say in front of you—you've heard me say it a thousand times—if I were President, this war would have never happened. We would have had a deal negotiated for you without having to go through what you've gone through.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But you—your soldiers have been unbelievably brave. We've given them great equipment, but they've—somebody has to use the equipment. They've been unbelievably brave, and we give them great credit. This was supposed to be over very quickly, and here we are 3 years later. So I give tremendous credit to your generals and your soldiers and yourself, in the sense that it's been very hard fighting, very tough fighting. They're great fighters. And you have to be very proud of them from that standpoint.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. I am very proud, of course.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. But now we want to get it over with. [Laughter] It's enough, right? We want to get it over with.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So it's an honor to have you here. Thank you very much for coming.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And an honor to have you. And please, if you'd like to say something.

context.text: President Zelenskyy. Yes. Thank you so much, Mr. President. Thank you for invitation.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: And really, I hope that this document—first document will be first step to real security guarantees for Ukraine, our people, our children. I really count on it.

context.text: And of course, we count that America will not stop support. Really, for us, it's very important to support and to continue it. I want to discuss it with details further during our conversation and, of course, the infrastructure or security guarantees, because, for today, I understand what Europe is ready to do, and of course, I want to discuss with you what United States will be ready to do.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: And I really count on your strong position to stop Putin. And you said that "Enough with the war." I think that is very important—been—to say these words to Putin at the very beginning—at the very beginning of war, because he is a killer and terrorist.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: But I hope that together we can stop him. But for us, it's very important to—you know, to save our country, our values, our freedom, and democracy. And of course, no compromises with a killer about our territories. But it will be later.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: And of course, I—what I wanted—you know we spoke about it by phone with you about the drones production. We have very good drones production. I think the best one in the world for today because of the war.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: Yes. And of course, we need very much the air defense. You have the best air defense in the world. And really, you helped us under attacks of Russians. context.text: Even after the war, we need our nation to be calm, that we are secured. So that's why we need this air shield.

context.text: And the last point—last, not least—about exchange—about our people and children. And you know that these crazy Russians—that they've stolen 20,000 of children—Ukrainian children. context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: We—by the way, Mr. President, we brought—we exchanged—we just released more than 4,000 warriors from Russian prison, but there are thousands more in the prison. I wanted to share with you some—some images how—it's—of just—can—I—can I now—

But it means we're going to be inside, and it's a big commitment from the United States, and we appreciate working with you very much, and we will continue to do that.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: We have had some very good discussions with Russia. I spoke with President Putin, and we're going to try and bring this to a close. That's something that you want and that he wants. We have to negotiate a deal, but we've started the confines of a deal, and I think something can happen.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: The big thing is the number of soldiers, mostly, at this point, but soldiers being killed. You're losing thousands of soldiers. On both sides, we're losing a lot of soldiers, and we want to see it stop. And we want to see the money get put to different kinds of use, like rebuilding—the rebuilding.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: And we're going to be working very hard, but we've had a lot of very good conversations. I will say, until we came along, the Biden administration didn't speak to Russia whatsoever. They didn't speak to anybody. They just allowed this to continue.

favorable_source_context.text: And I will say that—I'll say in front of you—you've heard me say it a thousand times—if I were President, this war would have never happened. We would have had a deal negotiated for you without having to go through what you've gone through.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: But you—your soldiers have been unbelievably brave. We've given them great equipment, but they've—somebody has to use the equipment. They've been unbelievably brave, and we give them great credit. This was supposed to be over very quickly, and here we are 3 years later. So I give tremendous credit to your generals and your soldiers and yourself, in the sense that it's been very hard fighting, very tough fighting. They're great fighters. And you have to be very proud of them from that standpoint.
