context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Northern Ireland/Ukraine/Russia

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. What does it say to you that the United States is recognized as having such an important role in the peace process, and yet half the parties from the Northern Ireland government have decided not to come to the St. Patrick's Day celebrations?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. They haven't—what?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. They haven't come over. They're boycotting the St. Patrick's Day celebrations in Ireland.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. What are they boycotting?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. They are talking about your position on Gaza as one of the reasons why——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Oh, I haven't heard that.

context.speaker: Q. ——
context.text: Q. ——they've decided to stay away.

context.speaker: Mixed
context.text: President Trump. I really haven't heard that. Look—— Prime Minister Martin. Could—could I just say, as a—— President Trump. Yes.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: Prime Minister Martin. ——to pay tribute to the President on the peace initiatives. The one thing we've learned in Ireland about the peace process that you've just spoken about—and I recall back in the early nineties when the first tentative steps to get peace in Ireland, people criticized people like John Hume or people like Albert Reynolds—the then-Taoiseach.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: But they kept going. And when we got that cease-fire in '93—okay, it took a number of years to get the comprehensive peace settlement, but, again, the guns, more or less, largely went silent.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: The war in Ukraine is a devastating war on young people. And I think that very simple, straightforward narrative——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. That's right.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: Prime Minister Martin. ——is to be commended. We all have children. We—I mean, we— shocked at the prospect of young people losing their lives in that number, be they Ukrainian, be

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: they Russian, whatever. Anything we can do to stop the violence, I think, is an extremely positive thing.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: And there will be all sorts of people having qualifications and all the rest of it. It's our job then to work on it and to try and build it—Europe, U.S., and every——

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I will say—and thank you for that. But I will say, last week, 2,500 young people died while we sit here and talk——

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: Prime Minister Martin. Yes.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. ——and while they talk about peace. But they've been talking about peace—this should have never happened. This war should have never happened. It would have never happened if I was President. That's what makes me more angry than anything else, because you've had far more people die than they report—then these people report——

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: Prime Minister Martin. The media report.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. ——for whatever reason. But you had far more people—the numbers are far more devastating. You'll find that out someday.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And it doesn't affect you very much. You're—they're not Irish, and they're not from my country. They're from Russia, mostly—almost all from Russia—and from Ukraine. And people could say: "Why are you doing this? Why are you involved in that?" Because they're—2,000 people a week are dying, and they have families, and they have mothers, and they have fathers, and they have sisters, and they have brothers and friends, and they're dying. And I've seen the pictures—the satellite pictures that we see all the time, and it looks like Gettysburg in its prime, because that was, they say, one of the most horrific battles ever.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You have kids lying all over these fields that are dead because the weapons today are unbelievable, between drones and various types of guns. I'm not even talking about—beyond that, with the—with the big babies. You understand what I mean.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: Prime Minister Martin. Yes.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I hate to even mention the name—the nuclear name. I hate to mention it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But you have weapons today that are so powerful. And I see kids—every week, I see pictures of kids laying all over the field, dead. They're dead. Beautiful kids, they're dead.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And they're not from here, and they're not from where you are, but he's working very hard. We're all working hard to get this thing finished. It's crazy. Over nothing, and it's not going to go anywhere. It's just a terrible situation.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I think we have a chance to get it done. So we've gotten——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. We've gotten half of it as a cease-fire. And if we can get Russia to stop, and then we have a full cease-fire, and I think it will never go back to war. I think something will happen.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.] Say it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: There wasn't a—from people sitting there, Democrats, there wasn't a hand clap. They're— nobody stood. They were just stone-faced. These people are sick. There's something wrong with them. There was no standing for anybody.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The only thing they liked is when they heard about the death taking place with Ukraine. That way—they were happy about that. They were happy about that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Well, Pocahontas was very happy. She's the one that was clapping—that's why I looked at her. I said, "Oh, it's Pocahontas." These people are sick. They don't know what's happening in the real world.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The Democrats have to get their act together, and if they don't vote, then what you're going to do is you're going to have taxes that are going to go through the roof. You're going to have a very bad time. You're going to have some very bad things happen, and people are going to blame the Democrats.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Russia/Nord Stream 2 Natural Gas Pipeline Between Russia and Germany/President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. You said earlier that it is now up to Russia, in terms of a cease-fire.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Is there anything you can do in terms of pressuring Russia or——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes.

context.speaker: Q. ——
context.text: Q. ——in terms of sanctions or—what can you do?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes, we can, but I hope it's not going to be necessary. Sure, we can pressure. We can do that with Russia.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Remember this: Russia took Georgia from Bush, right? They took Crimea from a man named Obama—Barack Hussein Obama, right? They're trying to take the whole thing from Biden. They're going for the whole ball of wax.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Who was the only one that ever took anything from? Trump. And in fact, I'm the one that stopped Nord Stream 2, the pipeline. The biggest pipeline anywhere in the world. I stopped it. It was dead. And then Biden got in, and he approved it. Nobody mentions that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: What I did to Russia was very tough. I was the toughest ever. But nope, they never took anything from me. They took them from Obama and Bush, and they took it from Sleepy Joe Biden. With Biden, they wanted to take the whole country, but I think I've stopped that, but we'll see.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But yes, there are things you could do that—that wouldn't be pleasant. In a financial sense— I can do things financially that would be very bad for Russia. I don't want to do that because I want to get peace. I want to see peace, and we'll see. But in a financial sense, yes, we could do things very bad for Russia. It would be devastating for Russia. But I don't want to do that because I want to see peace.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And we're getting close to maybe getting something done. We've got Ukraine done.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And as you know, I've always said that Ukraine might have been the more difficult party. You saw—you were here a week ago when some interesting things happened. I had somebody that didn't seem to want peace. Now he's agreed to peace. So we'll see what happens.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, what about on Gaza?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Hey.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Brian [Brian Glenn, Real America's Voice]. Brian.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Yes, thanks.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Thank you.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. First, we'll congratulate you on your lower inflation core rates.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Thank you.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Gas prices going down, airline prices going down.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: This is for our Irish gentleman here, if I can see him real quickly. Welcome to the United States. You look great.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: Prime Minister Martin. Thank you.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Nice suit. [Laughter]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. That's a—now you're feeling good. He knows.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: Prime Minister Martin. That's compliments too.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. President Trump ran on MAGA—"Make America Great Again." If you could run on MIGA, "Make Ireland Great Again," what would your number-one issue be for people in Ireland right now to make your country stronger?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: And then I've got a two-part question to that as well.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: Prime Minister Martin. Yes. The number-one issue in Ireland is housing, to be honest. And I think it was correctly pointed out, we've got to build more houses. We've got to build them faster to give the young people of Ireland an opportunity to afford to buy a house or to afford to rent a house.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: We have a lot of other good things happening. That's my number-one priority.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Wonderful. Thank you.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Are you trying to infer, Mr. President——

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Russia/Ukraine

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, thank you so much. You spoke to Vladimir Putin for quite a while on the phone.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. So I want to know your assessment. When you take this deal to him now, what do you— how do you assess the chances of Putin saying yes?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I have no assessment, and I don't go by chances.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I think it makes sense for Russia. A lot of downside for Russia too. And we have a very complex situation solved on one side, pretty much solved. We've also discussed land and other things that, you know, go with it. We're not just doing it and saying "cease-fire." We don't know what's happening.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We know the areas of land we're talking about, whether it's pulled back or not pulled back.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You know, we've discussed a lot of the details of what has to go because we don't want to be wasting time.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We don't want to be wasting time while people are dying. I mean, as we're sitting here, you probably had two people die on that very open field. You know, it's dead flat. It's great farmland, and it's dead flat. There's no protection.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The only thing that stops a bullet is a human body, and these are bodies that are young people, and they're stopping a lot of bullets, because a lot of bullets are flying across those level fields—dead flat, no protection whatsoever. It is a disaster.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And so I hope he's going to have a cease-fire. [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. And you are using—you are using the American leverage to get a lot of political issues that you want across, right?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, I don't want to get into that.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. And I'm wondering——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. But if I had to, I'm the only one that's dealt with him successfully.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Everyone else went through it. Bush didn't deal with him successfully. He dealt with him terribly. He got ripped off.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And Obama was a disaster. You know——

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/U.S. Security Assistance

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. So what leverage do you, sir——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. ——they had with Obama—he gave them sheets, and I gave them anti- tank missiles. You know that, right? It's called Javelin. You know the Javelin? I'm the one that gave them the Javelins. People don't say that. And then, they say, "Oh, Trump has a great relationship with Russia."

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. But so what leverage do you have to use? But—Mr. President——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I'm the one that gave them the Javelins. Obama gave them sheets. That's an expression. He gave sheets; I gave Javelins. So——

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, how worried—how worried should the—how worried should the undocumented Irish be about your administration that you don't round them up and send them home again?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Oh, I think the Irish love Trump. We won the Irish with a tremendous amount of vote. I want to thank you very much. We won in the eighties with Irish. I got the Irish vote.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I think I have it locked up pretty good, unless I did something very stupid, like drained your company—your wonderful place of all of its companies. If I drained Ireland of all the companies—maybe I'd lose the Irish vote. I don't know. [Laughter] But right now—no, I love—I love your—I love it. I've been there many times, as you know.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Martin
context.text: Prime Minister Martin. Yes.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. And we don't want to do anything to hurt Ireland. We want to—but we do want fairness, and—and he understands that.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, on the markets. You often——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. No, that's enough, Kelly. Thank you.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, is there anything that the Taoiseach could say to you today that would dissuade you from going ahead with the 25-percent tariffs on EU goods?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I can't hear.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. We're going to be discussing a lot of things. Obviously, we'll be discussing what's happening with respect to Ukraine and Russia.

context.text: At this moment, we have people talking in Russia. We have representatives over there— Steve Witkoff and others. And they're in very serious discussions. context.text: Secretary General Rutte. No.

context.speaker: Trump

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: It's also a tremendous cost to the United States and to other countries. And it's something that would have never happened if I were President, and it makes me very angry to see that it did happen. But it happened, and we have to stop it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And Mark has done some really good work over the last week. We've been working together, and he's done some really good work. So I'm very happy about that.

context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: They're not there. We need to do more. But I really want to work together with you in a runup to The Hague summit to make sure that we will have a NATO which is really reinvigorated under your leadership. And we are getting there.

context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: We also discussed defense production, because we need to produce more weaponry. We are not doing enough—not in the U.S., not in Europe. And we are lagging behind when you compare to the Russians and the Chinese. And you have a huge defense industrial base, Europeans buying

context.text: —four times more here than the other—the other way around, which is good, because you have a strong defense industry.

context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: But we need to do more there to make sure that we ramp up production and kill the red tape.

context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: So I would love to work with you on that.

context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: And finally, Ukraine, you broke the deadlock. As you said, all the killing, the young people dying, cities getting destroyed. context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: So, well, the Hague is my hometown. I'd love to host you there in the summer and work together to make sure that——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. We'll do that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And now we have to use it wisely. And we have to get this war over with. And you'll be back to a normal—much more normal life.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And maybe we're close. We're getting words that things are going okay in Russia, and it doesn't mean anything until we hear what the final outcome is.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But they have very serious discussions going on right now with President Putin and others. And hopefully, they all want to end this nightmare. It's a nightmare. context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: Secretary General Rutte. It's so terrible.

context.speaker: Trump

context.speaker: Trump

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So we, hopefully, are going to be in a good position sometime today to have a good idea. We'll have—we know where we are with Ukraine, and we are getting good signals outside of Russia as to where we are with Russia, and hopefully, they'll do the right thing.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: It's a really—humanity—we're talking about humanity. We're not talking about the money. But then you add the money to it, and you know, hundreds of billions of dollars is being spent and, really, wasted so unnecessarily. It should have never happened.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So it's an honor to have you here. They picked a great gentleman. I'll tell you, that was—I was so happy to hear, because you had somebody—Stoltenberg was really good. And you have somebody that's going to do an incredible job. And I was so much in favor of you, you have no idea.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Please, go ahead.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Vladimir——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Sorry. Sorry, Mary [Mary Bruce, ABC News]. Steve Witkoff's trip to Moscow, you spoke about it. What sort of agreement do you hope he comes away from there with?

context.text: There's a power plant involved—you know, a very big power plant involved. Who's going to get the power plant and who's going to get this and that. And so, you know, it's—it's not an easy process.

prompt_links.speaker: Q. ——
prompt_links.quote: And for President Trump. Kremlin yesterday said if you are going to Beijing in September, they wouldn't rule out a meeting between you and President Putin. Is such a meeting possible? And how soon do you plan to visit China?

context.speaker: Q. ——
context.text: Mr. President Marcos. Next year, Philippines is going to be the rotating chair of ASEAN. I wonder: How do you plan to balance your relationship between the United States and China?

context.speaker: Q. ——
context.text: And for President Trump. Kremlin yesterday said if you are going to Beijing in September, they wouldn't rule out a meeting between you and President Putin. Is such a meeting possible? And how soon do you plan to visit China?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, we have a lot of meetings possible. President Xi has invited me to China, and we'll probably be doing that in the not-too-distant future, a little bit out, but not too distant. And I've been invited by a lot of people, and we'll make those decisions pretty soon.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Please.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Convicted Sex Offender Ghislaine Maxwell/Deputy Attorney General Todd Blanche/Past Investigation Into Russian 2016 Presidential Election Interference

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, do you support the Justice Department seeking a new interview with Ghislaine Maxwell? And did you urge the Attorney General to seek one?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I don't know anything about it. They're going to, what, meet her?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. They're going to—there's—your Deputy Attorney General is—reached out to Ghislaine Maxwell's attorney asking for a new interview.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes, I don't know about it——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. She has said she——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. ——but I think it's something that would be—sounds appropriate to do, yeah.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Do you have any concern that your Deputy Attorney General, who's your former attorney, would be conducting the interview, given your relationship——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. No, I——

context.speaker: Q. ——
context.text: Q. ——your past relationship with Epstein?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. He's very talented person. He's very smart. I didn't know that they were going to do it. I don't really follow that too much. It's sort of a witch hunt—just a continuation of the witch hunt.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The witch hunt that you should be talking about is they caught President Obama absolutely cold—Tulsi Gabbard. What they did to this country in 2016—starting in 2016, but going up all the way—going up to 2020 of the election, they tried to rig the election, and they got caught. And there should be very severe consequences for that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You know, when we caught Hillary Clinton, I said, "You know what, let's not go too far here. It's the ex-wife of a President." And I thought it was sort of terrible. And I let her off the

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: hook, and I'm very happy I did. But it's time to start—after what they did to me, and whether it's right or wrong, it's time to go after people.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Obama has been caught directly. So people say, "Oh, you know, a group." It's not a group. It's Obama. His orders are on the paper. The papers are signed. The papers came right out of their office. They sent everything to be highly classified.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Well, the highly classified has been released. And what they did in 2016 and in 2020 is very criminal. It's criminal at the highest level. So that's really the things you should be talking about.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I know nothing about the other, but I think it's appropriate that they do go.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: 2016 Presidential Election/Intelligence Community Assessment of Russian Election Interference/Oval Office Decorations/News Media/Illegal Immigration

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. May I ask you about that, Mr. President?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Tulsi Gabbard has submitted a criminal referral to the Department of Justice. From your perspective, who should the DOJ target as part of their investigation? What specific figures in the Obama administration?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, based on what I read—and I read pretty much what you read—it would be President Obama. He started it. And Biden was there with him, and Comey was there, and Clapper—the whole group was there—Brennan. They were all there. The—in a room. Right here. This was the room.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: This is much more beautiful than it was then, but that's okay. I have nice pictures up. They came out of the vaults. They were in there for a hundred years. This is much more beautiful.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We have the Declaration of Independence now in the room, which wasn't here. I guess people didn't feel too good about putting it here, but I do.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But you know what? If you look at that—those papers, they have him stone cold, and it was President Obama. It wasn't lots of people all over the place. It was them too, but the leader of the gang was President Obama—Barack Hussein Obama. Have you heard of him?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And except for the fact that he gets shielded by the press for his entire life, that's the one they—look, he's guilty. It's not a question—you know, I like to say, "Let's give it time." It's there. He's guilty.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: They—this was treason. This was every word you can think of. They tried to steal the election. They tried to obfuscate the election. They did things that nobody's ever even imagined, even in other countries.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You've seen some pretty rough countries. [Laughter] This man has seen some pretty rough countries, but you've never seen anything like it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And we have all of the documents. And from what Tulsi told me, she's got thousands of additional documents coming.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So President Obama, it was his concept, his idea, but he also got it from Crooked Hillary Clinton. Crooked as a $3 bill. Hillary Clinton and her group, the Democrats, spent $12 million to Christopher Steele to write up a report that was a total fake report. Took 2 years to figure that out, but it came out that it was a total fake report. It was made-up fiction, and they used that—now, the one thing they weren't able to do was to get—and probably the only thing I respect about the press in years, is the press refused to write it before the election. They refused to put it in. The Steele report was a disaster. All lies. All fabrication. All admitted—an admitted fraud.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: She paid $12 million—and the Democrats—for that report to a wise guy named Christopher Steele. He wrote a phony report, and they wanted to get that report in before the election.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I'll tell you what—I talk about it all the time: the fake news, how bad it is. But, in this case, they wouldn't do it. They saw it, they read it, and they said, "We don't believe it." And it was only after—substantially—like a month and a half after the election, that it got printed. And it was a big whisper—it was just like a bang of nothing, because the election had ended.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: If that report had gotten published by the New York Times or somebody—and I respect the Times for maybe only this, because they're crooked as you can be. They're a terrible paper—a crooked, corrupt paper. But for this one moment, they said: "This is bullshit. We can't put this in." And neither could any other paper—Wall Street Journal is a lousy paper—a very, very dishonest paper. As you see, I'm suing them for a lot of money because they do things very badly. It's a really—it's got a nice name, but it's really—in my opinion, it's a terrible paper, and it can be corrupt.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But just so you know, they didn't take the Steele report. It was the dossier. Remember the famous dossier? I called it "the fake news dossier." The news wouldn't publish it, and I'm amazed. They had 2½ months. It was finished. Two and a half months. That was supposed to be what was going to happen, and it got published a couple of months after the election, and frankly, nobody cared too much about it. But that was a big thing.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: No, no, we caught Hillary Clinton. We caught Barack Hussein Obama. They're the ones, and then you have many, many people under them. Susan Rice—they're all there. The names are all there.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I guess they figured they're going to put this in classified information and nobody will ever see it again, but it doesn't work that way. And it's the most unbelievable thing I think I've ever read.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So you ought to take a look at that and stop talking about nonsense, because this is big stuff.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Never has a thing like this happened in the history of our country.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And by the way, it morphed into the 2020 race. And the 2020 race was rigged, and it was a rigged election. And because it was rigged, we have millions of people in our country. We have—we had inflation. We solved the inflation problem.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But millions and millions of people came into our country because of that and people that shouldn't have been—people from gangs and from jails and from mental institutions, people that we don't want in our country and people that we're getting out, dangerous people—11,888 murderers. Many of them—50 percent—more than 50 percent murdered more than one person.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I hate to say this with such a distinguished guest, but you know, they asked me a question. I got to answer the question.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: No. Barack Hussein Obama is the ringleader. Hillary Clinton was right there with him and so was Sleepy Joe Biden. And so were the rest of them: Comey, Clapper, the whole group. And they tried to rig an election, and they got caught. And then they did rig the election in 2020, and then, because I knew I won that election by a lot, I did it a third time and I won in a landslide—every swing State, won the popular vote. But I won that all the same way in 2020, and look at the damage that was caused.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Okay.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: 2024 Assassination Attempt on Former President Donald J. Trump in Butler, Pennsylvania/U.S. Secret Service/Intelligence Community Assessment of Russian Election Interference/Former President Joseph R. Biden, Jr./

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. A least—I've also got a question. I find it a very interesting world that we know more about two people at a Coldplay concert just hours after that viral video than we know of Thomas Crooks 1 year after attempting to assassinate you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. What is holding back the investigation on Thomas Crooks?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, they've reported to me, and they've told me things, and they really say they haven't found anything that was abnormal.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I would say this: The Secret Service was very brave, because they—you know, they were right there, and they jumped on me. They made a mistake. They should have had somebody on that roof, and they should have had communication with the local police, who also—I mean, they did a very good job, but they made some mistakes.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And we have a whole different group of people now. It's just—I don't think any—look, anything can happen, but I think we have the best people anywhere in the world right now, and I think they've learned.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And you know, they went into him very—you know, in great detail. They gave me the whole thing. And what can I do? They say that it was just a nutjob that was looking to do this. And I spoke with the FBI—the new FBI. I spoke to the FBI. If it was the old FBI, I wouldn't have believed a thing they said, because the old FBI under Comey was crooked as hell. He was one of the most crooked.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Everybody should read the Horowitz report. Unfortunately, Bill Barr didn't use it, but the Horowitz report—not appointed by me. It was a report on Comey and the FBI. It is one of the worst shots at a human being I think I've ever seen. In fact, the New York Times did an editorial that was one of the worst editorials I've ever seen about anybody. That was about Comey. You ought go back and get—and Barr didn't use it because he didn't have the guts to use it, or something happened. I don't know. And too bad.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: He went to Mr. Durham instead of using—instead of doing the Durham, all they had to use was the Horowitz report. And I always felt badly for Horowitz, frankly, because he's a Democrat, I guess. He was appointed by a Democrat. But that report has gotten lost, and it shouldn't be lost.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You should all go back. It should be mandatory reading. Go back and read the Horowitz report on Comey and his cronies, and you'll see exactly—I'm—we're going to add that to all the stuff that we found. It just confirms it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But what we found is even more so, and we found absolute—this isn't, like, evidence or the—this is, like, proof—irrefutable proof that Obama was seditious, that Obama led—was trying to lead a coup. And it was with Hillary Clinton, with all these other people, but Obama headed it up.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And you know, I get a kick when I hear—everyone talks about people I never even heard of. "It was this one." No, no. It was Obama. He headed it up. And it says so right in the papers. Got everything. Got everything.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: This is the biggest scandal in the history of our country, and it really goes on to even the autopen, because it all relates to the same thing. It all started—the same sick minds. You have an autopen, which is a tremendous—where we don't have a President, we have an autopen that signs everything. [Laughter]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I'll bet you sign everything. You don't have autopens.

context.speaker: President Marcos
context.text: President Marcos. No, I do not. [Laughter]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Everybody—who doesn't sign? You're the President of a country. But it's all that whole thing. Leading right up to the—to the end of it is the autopen. And the autopen was used by people, and Biden knew nothing about it. Biden knew nothing about it. They were signing documents that he knew nothing about.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: As an example, they released the "Unselect Committee" of liability. The "Unselect Committee" spent 2 years grilling everybody, and then they destroyed all the evidence. You know why? Because the evidence made them guilty. And he gave them all a pardon. The—Cheney, all the—all the scum that was on the "Unselect Committee"—Crying Adam Kinzinger and Democrats. And he gave them a pardon.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Do you have something else? Go ahead. [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: 2016 Presidential Election/Russian Election Interference

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. You talked a lot about the severe consequences that those who were involved in the Russia hoax must face. In your view, sir, what are the next steps now that these documents are out there and Tulsi Gabbard released them?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, the Justice Department would have to act, and we have a very competent, very good, very loyal-to-our-country person in Pam Bondi. Very respected. And she—it's going to be her decision.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. And just a follow-up to that, sir. Kristi Noem was in New York City visiting an off-duty CBP officer who was allegedly shot this weekend by an illegal alien who came into the country during the previous administration.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Right.

context.text: Russia/Ukraine/President Trump's Meeting With President Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin of Russia

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Related, just because you mentioned the elusive peace in Ukraine.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Right.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Who is holding up this Ukraine cease-fire summit? Is it Putin, or is it Zelenskyy?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Russia, as you know, lost almost 25,000 over the last month and a half, and Ukraine lost just a small number fewer. It's a lot of people are dying.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I think we're getting very close. And we're going to be announcing, later on, we're going to have a meeting with Russia. We'll start off with Russia, and we'll announce a location. context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. And I completely understand that. Just——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes, please. Go ahead.

context.speaker: Reporter

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I think—you know, I think that a lot of things happened recently that would make this go forward. context.text: Nobel Peace Prize/Ukraine/Russia

context.text: And I'm not politicking for it. I have a lot of people that are. I know—I mean, I read the same things as you do. But it would be a great honor, certainly, but I would never politic.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I'm not doing it for that. I'm doing it because of—I really—number one, I want to save lives.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: That's why I'm involved so much with Ukraine and Russia. It's saving lives of Russians and Ukrainians. I'm—it's not American lives.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Now, I would say this, that war could have escalated in some-—something much—that could have been a world war. I think if we didn't come, Ukraine-Russia would have ended up being a world war, and I stopped that. That stopped.

context.text: Now the only question is: When is it going to be settled? And it could be very soon. But when is it going to be—but that would have been a world war. context.text: Q. Your predecessor, Mr. President——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I don't think people talk about that now because they don't see it anymore, but we brought it down a long way. And it could have gone—it could have escalated to a level that you people would have been very unhappy with.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Yes.

Getting that one settled, I think you'd agree, that was a big one.

context.text: President Putin. Mr. President, ladies and gentlemen, our negotiations have been held in a constructive atmosphere of mutual respect. We have very thorough negotiations that were quite useful.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: I would like to thank, once again, my American counterpart for the proposal to travel out here to Alaska. It only makes sense that we've met here because our countries, though separated by the oceans, are close neighbors.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: So, when we've met, when I came out of the plane and I said: "Good afternoon, dear neighbor. Very good to see you in good health and to see you alive," I think that is very neighborly. And I think that's some kind words that we can say to each other

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: We're separated by the Strait of Bering, though there are two islands only between the Russian island and the U.S. island. They're only 4 kilometers apart. We are close neighbors, and it's a fact.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: It's also important that Alaska has to do with our common heritage—common history between Russia and the U.S. And many positive events have to do with that territory.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: Still, there is tremendous cultural heritage back from the Russian America. For example, Orthodox churches and a lot of—more than 700 geographical names of Russian origin.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: During the Second World War, it was here in Alaska that was the origin of the legendary air bridge for the supply of military aircraft and other equipment under the Lend-Lease program.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: It was a dangerous and treacherous route over the vast emptiness of ice. However, the pilots of both countries did everything to bring closer the victory. They risked their lives, and they gave it all for the common victory.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: I was just in the city of Magadan in Russia, and there is a memorial there dedicated to the Russian and the U.S. pilots. And there are two flags: the U.S. flag and the Russian flag. And I know that here, as well, there is such a memorial.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: There is a military burial place several kilometers away from here. The Soviet pilots are buried there who died during that dangerous mission. We're thankful to the citizens and the Government of the U.S. for carefully taking care of their memory. I think that's very worthy and noble.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: We'll always remember other historical examples when our countries defeated common enemies together in the spirit of battle camaraderie and allyship. They supported each other and facilitated each other.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: I am sure that this heritage will help us rebuild and foster mutually beneficial and equal ties at this new stage, even during the hardest conditions.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: It is known that there have been no summits between Russia and the U.S. for 4 years, and that's a long time. This time was very hard for bilateral relations. And let's be frank, they have fallen to the lowest point since this—the cold war. I think that's not benefiting our countries and the world as a whole.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: It is apparent that, sooner or later, we had to amend the situation to move on from the confrontation to dialogue. And in this case, a personal meeting between the heads of state has been long overdue, naturally, under the condition of serious and painstaking work, and this work has been done.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: In general, me and President Trump have very good direct contact. We've spoken multiple times. We spoke frankly on the phone. And Special Envoy of the President, Mr. Witkoff, traveled out to Russia several times. Our advisers and heads of foreign ministries kept in touch all the time.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: And you know fully well that one of the central issues was the situation around Ukraine. We see the strive of the administration and President Trump personally to help facilitate the resolution of the Ukrainian conflict. And his strive to get to the crux of the matter, to understand this history is precious. As I've said, the situation in Ukraine has to do with fundamental threats to our security.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: Moreover, we've always considered the Ukrainian nation—and I've said it multiple times—a brotherly nation, however strange it may sound in these conditions. We have the same roots, and everything that's happening is a tragedy for us and terrible wound. Therefore, the country is sincerely interested in putting an end to it.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: At the same time, we are convinced that in order to make the settlement lasting and long term, we need to eliminate all the primary roots, the primary causes of that conflict—and we've said it multiple times—to consider all legitimate concerns of Russia and to reinstate a just balance of security in Europe and in world on the whole.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: And I agree with President Trump, as he has said today, that, naturally, the security of Ukraine should be ensured as well. Naturally, we are prepared to work on that.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: I would like to hope that the agreement that we've reached together will help us bring closer that goal and will pave the path towards peace in Ukraine.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: We expect that Kyiv and European capitals will perceive that constructively and that they won't throw a wrench in the works. They will not make any attempts to use some backroom dealings to conduct provocations to torpedo the nascent progress.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: Incidentally, when the new administration came to power, bilateral trade started to grow. This is still very symbolic. Still, we have a growth of 20 percent. As I've said, we have a lot of dimensions for joint work.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: It is clear that the U.S. and Russian investment and business potential—cooperation has tremendous potential. Russia and the U.S. can offer each other so much in trade, digital, high-tech, and in space exploration.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: We see that Arctic cooperation is also very possible, and our international context, for example, between the far east of Russia and the west coast of the U.S.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: Overall, it's very important for our countries to turn the page, to go back to cooperation. It is symbolic that not far away from here, the border between Russia and the U.S., there is a so-called International Date Line. I think you can step over, literally, from yesterday into tomorrow. And I hope that we'll succeed in that in political sphere.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: I would like to thank President Trump for our joint work, for the well-wishing and trustworthy tone of our conversation. It's important that both sides are result-oriented, and we see that the President of the U.S. has a very clear idea of what he would like to achieve. He sincerely cares about prosperity of his nation. Still, he understands that Russia has its own national interests.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: I expect that today's agreements will be the starting point not only for the solution of the Ukrainian issue, but also will help us bring back businesslike and pragmatic relations between Russia and the U.S.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: And in the end, I would like to add one more thing. I'd like to remind you that in 2022, during the last contact with a previous administration, I tried to convince my previous American colleague that it should not—the situation should not be brought to the point of no return when it would come to hostilities. And I said it quite directly back then that it's a big mistake.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: Today, when President Trump saying that if he was the President back then, there would be no war, and I'm quite sure that it would indeed be so. I can confirm that.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: I think that overall, me and President Trump have built a very good, businesslike, and trustworthy contact. And I have every reason to believe that moving down this path, we can come—and the sooner, the better—to the end of the conflict in Ukraine.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: Thank you. Thank you.

context.text: President Trump. Well, thank you very much, Mr. President. That was very profound. And I will say that I believe we had a very productive meeting. There were many, many points that we agreed on—most of them, I would say. A couple of big ones that we haven't quite gotten there, but we've made some headway.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So there's no deal until there's a deal. I will call up NATO in a little while. I will call up the various people that I think are appropriate. context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But we have some of our really great leaders. They've been doing a phenomenal job. We also have some tremendous Russian business representatives here. And I think, you know, everybody wants to deal with us. We've become the hottest country anywhere in the world in a very short period of time. And we look forward to that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We look forward to dealing—we're going to try and get this over with. We really made some great progress today. I've always had a fantastic relationship with President Putin, with Vladimir. We had many, many tough meetings, good meetings. context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I think he's probably seen things like that during the course of his career. He's seen it all. But we had to put up with the "Russia, Russia, Russia" hoax. But it made it harder for us to deal as a country in terms of the business and all of the things that we'd like to have dealt with. But we'll have a good chance when this is over.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So, just to put it very quickly, I'm going to start making a few phone calls and tell them what happened. But we had an extremely productive meeting, and many points were agreed to. There are just a very few that are left. Some are not that significant. One is probably the most significant. But we have a very good chance of getting there. We didn't get there, but we have a very good chance of getting there.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I would like to thank President Putin and his entire team, whose faces—who I know, in many cases—otherwise, other than that, whose faces I get to see all the time in the newspapers. You're very—you're almost as famous as the boss, but—especially this one right over here. [Laughter]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But we had some good meetings over the years, right? Good, productive meetings over the years, and we hope to have that in the future. But let's do the most productive one right now.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We're going to stop, really, 5-, 6-, 7,000—thousands of people a week from being killed.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And President Putin wants to see that as much as I do.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So, again, Mr. President, I'd like to thank you very much, and we'll speak to you very soon and probably see you again very soon.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Thank you very much, Vladimir.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: [At this point, President Putin spoke briefly in English as follows.] President Putin. And next time in Moscow.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Oh, that's an interesting one. [Laughter] I don't know. I'll get a little heat on that one. But I could see it possibly happening.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Thank you very much, Vladimir.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: President Putin. Thank you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. And thank you all. Thank you. Thank you.

context.speaker: President Putin
context.text: President Putin. Thank you so much.
