context.text: We have, I guess, the seven—seven very powerful leaders from Europe, and we're going to be meeting with them right after this meeting. And thank you very much for being here.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. Thank you so much, Mr. President. If I can, first of all——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Please.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. ——thank you for invitation, and thank you very much for your efforts—personal efforts to stop killings and stop this war. Thank you. And using this opportunity, many thanks to your wife, First Lady of the United States. She sent a letter to Putin about our children—abducted children. And my wife, she—the First Lady of Ukraine——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Oh.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. ——she gave the letter——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. That's very nice.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. ——it's not to you—to your wife.

context.speaker: Mixed
context.text: President Trump. Oh. [Laughter] I want it. I want it. President Zelenskyy. Yes. [Laughter] Yes, yes, yes. So we are saying this sensitive topic.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: [At this point, President Trump held up the letter.] Yes. Yes, please.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: And thanks to our partners and that you supported this format, that, after our meeting, we're going to have leaders who are around us—the U.K. and France, Germany, Italy, Finland, EU, NATO—I mean, all—all partners around Ukraine supporting us. Thanks them and thank you very much for invitation.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: Thank you. Thank you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Thank you very much for being here.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Russi/Ukraine

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Thank you, President Trump.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: So, President Zelenskyy, you say, in a post on X today, "Russia must end this war, which it itself started."

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: President Trump, you say, "President Zelenskyy of Ukraine can end the war with Russia almost immediately, if he wants to."

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Which is it?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes, I think that's true. I think they'll—we're going to have a meeting. I think we're going to—if everything works out well today, we'll have a trilat. And I think there will be a reasonable chance of ending the war when we do that.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. And is this the end of the road for American support for Ukraine? Is today's meeting deal or no deal?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I can never say that. It's never the end of the road. People are being killed, and we want to stop that. So I would not say it's the end of the road.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: No, I think we have a good chance of doing it. It's been almost 4 years now that—a lot of people were killed last week. A lot of people last week. I mean, millions of people killed, but a lot of people last week, for whatever reason. A big number. A lot of soldiers, both—on both sides.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I know the President, I know myself, and I believe Vladimir Putin wants to see it ended.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. And as you—you met with Putin on Friday. Today you've got President Zelenskyy here. As you listen to Russia and Ukraine, which side has the better cards right now?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, I don't want to say that. I'm just going to—I'm just here to be—look, this isn't my war. This is Joe Biden's war. He's the one that had a lot to do with this happening, and we want to get it ended. And we want it to end good for everybody. We want it to end good. The people of Ukraine have suffered incredibly. Incredibly.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters began asking questions at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. And to that point, President—President Zelenskyy—President Zelenskyy, are you prepared to keep sending Ukrainian troops to their deaths for another couple years, or are you going to agree to redraw the maps?

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. Thank you for your question. So, first of all, you know we live under, each day, attacks. You know that today have been a lot of attacks and a lot of wounded people. And a child was dead, small one—one year and a half. So we need to stop this war, to stop Russia, and we need support—American and European partners.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: We will do our best for this. So—and I think we—we show that we are strong people, and we supported the idea of the United States, of—personally of President Trump, to stop this war, to make diplomatic way of finishing this war. And we are ready for trilateral, as President said. This is a good signal about trilateral. I think this is very good.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: Thank you.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.] President Trump. Go ahead.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/U.S. Security Assistance

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Yes. If the peace deal will be achieved, are you going to be willing to send American peacekeepers to Ukraine?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, we're going to work with Ukraine, we're going to work with everybody, and we're going to make sure that, if there's peace, the peace is going to stay long term. This is very long term. We're not talking about a 2-year peace and then we end up in this mess again. We're going to make sure that everything is good. We'll work with Russia. We're going to work with Ukraine. And we're going to make sure it works.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I think if we can get to peace, it's going to work. I have no doubt about it. [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Following up on that, any—your team has talked about——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Please, go ahead.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/U.S. Security Assistance

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Your team has talked about security guarantees. Could that involve U.S. troops? Would you rule that out in the future?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. We'll let you know that maybe later today. We're meeting with seven great leaders of great countries also, and we'll be talking about that. They'll all be involved. But there'll be a lot of help. When it comes to security, there's going to be a lot of help. It's going to be good.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: They are first line of defense because they're there. They're Europe. But we're going to help them out also. We'll be involved. Yes.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Please.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Russia/President Trump's Foreign Policy

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, Vladimir Putin mentioned the—that the war will not end without addressing the root causes of this war. Do you—have you had an understanding what are the root causes of this war?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, look, the war is going to end. When it ends, I can't tell you. But the war is going to end. And this gentleman wants it to end, and Vladimir Putin wants it to end. I think the whole world is tired of it. And we're going to get it ended.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: It was—you know, I've done six wars. I've ended six wars. And I thought this maybe would be the easiest one. [Laughter] And it's not the easiest one. It's a tough one. A lot of—a lot of reasons for it, and they'll be talking about it for a long time, but they'll be talking about the others.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Look, India-Pakistan. We're talking about big places. When you look at—you just take a look at some of these wars. You—go to Africa and take a look at that: Rwanda and the Congo— Republic of the Congo. That's been going on for 31 years.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And so we've done a total of six, and we really have six, not including the fact that we obliterated—and it turned out to be a total obliteration—the nuclear in—as you saw, the nuclear—the future nuclear capability of Iran.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And this one, I think we're going to get solved also. I think—I feel confident we're going to get it solved.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. [Inaudible]—guarantees, sir, like your Special Envoy put forward?

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Please.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Russia

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Me? President Trump, do you think it's fair to—for Ukraine and for Russia to achieve a lasting and a durable peace if Ukraine cedes its territories that Russia hasn't yet conquered? Do you think it's a fair peace for Ukraine?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. We're going to have a lasting peace, just to answer the first part of your question. We're going to have a lasting peace. I hope it's going to be immediately. I hope it doesn't have to go on, and I think people—the whole world is going to be very happy when that's announced.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Yes, please.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: First Lady Melania Trump's Interest in the Ukraine-Russia Conflict

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President—you posted on social media, Mr. President, a very touching letter from the First Lady, and the letter was hand-delivered to President Putin. And it calls for an end to the war, essentially, because of the children and the children's future. Why did the first lady feel that letter was necessary? Was it because she believes that Mr. Putin is the aggressor in the war? Is a similar letter being delivered—hand-delivered to President Zelenskyy?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. So the First Lady felt very strongly. She's watched the same thing that you watch and that I watch. I see things that you don't get to see, and it's horrible.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But when—she's got a great love of children. She has a wonderful son that she loves probably more than anybody, including me, I hate to say it. But she loves her son. She loves children. And she hates to see—she hates to see something like this happening, and that goes for other wars too.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I mean, she sees the—the heartbreak, the parents, the funerals that you see on television— always funerals. We want to see something other than funerals.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: No, she felt—it was a beautiful letter. He—it was very well received by him. And she did ask me to say—you know, she would love to see this end. She would love to see it end. And she says it very openly, very proudly, and with great sorrow, because so many people have been killed.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Yes.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, last week—last week, Mr. President——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Brian [Brian Glenn, Real America's Voice]. Go ahead, Brian.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Yes. Yes, sir. I've got a question for each of you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. First of all is, President Zelenskyy, you look fabulous in that suit.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I said the same thing.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. Good to see you.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. You look—you look good.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I said the same thing.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Yes. It looks good on you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Isn't that nice? That's the one that attacked you last time. [Laughter] See, now he's a——

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. I remember the—[laughter]——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Yes.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. ——post.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. I apologize to you. But you look wonderful.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: No, my first question for you, President Zelenskyy——

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. But you are in the same suit. [Laughter]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Well——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I think it's——

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. You see, I changed. You are not.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. That's pretty good.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Maybe yours is much better than mine.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. Yes, please.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Russia/Elections During Military Conflict

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Real quickly, upon peace—God willing you get peace—are you open to holding an election in your country?

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. Yes, of course. We are open for election, yes. We have to do safety circumstances and a little bit we need to work in the Parliament, because during the war, you can't have elections. But we can do security. We need, maybe—how to say—we need a truce, yes, everywhere—in the battlefield, in the sky, in the sea—yes, to make possible for people to do democratic, open, legal elections.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: So we aren't ready——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. So you say during the war, you can't have elections.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. So——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. So, let me just see, 3½ years from now—so, you mean, if we happen to be in a war with somebody, no more elections? Oh, that's good. [Laughter] I wonder what the—I wonder what the fake news is going to say.

context.speaker: Mixed
context.text: President Zelenskyy. You like this idea? President Trump. No, no. This is very—— President Zelenskyy. Oh, no, no, no.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But you know, in solving all of these wars, they don't even write about it. You know, I solved major wars. I've solved wars that have been going on for 31, 35, and 37, and a couple of quicker ones—one that was going to go into a full-blown deal very quickly. You know what—the one I'm talking about. It was a big one. But they don't even write about that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: No matter what I do, no matter what—and you know, this is not anything to do with you. It's probably to your advantage, in a certain way. But no matter what I do, no matter what deal I make, from my standpoint, you'll come out good, maybe President Putin will come out good, but they'll say, "Trump was absolutely horrible." It's just that—and I've lived with that for a long time. I've lived with it since just before the first election.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I used to get great publicity. Now I get the worst publicity anyone's ever gotten in office. But I won in a landslide, so the people understand. They're the only ones that count, ultimately.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But I've also had great reporters. I've had journalists that are very good.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But it's very sad when you do the right thing—as an example, they said, "Because of the fact that Vladimir Putin came to American soil, this was a tremendous defeat for Donald Trump." No, it was really wonderful that he did it. It was a hard thing for him to do, to be honest with you. It was the opposite of what they said, but they said it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Now, if he didn't come, they'd say that was also bad for Trump. You know, there's no way. And there's just a great dishonesty of the press, and I think that's why it's lost its credibility. You know, its credibility is at an alltime low.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We have a thing going on right now in DC. We went from the most unsafe place anywhere to a place that now people—friends are calling me up, Democrats are calling me up, and they're saying: "Sir, I want to thank you. My wife and I went out to dinner last night for the first time in 4 years, and Washington, DC, is safe, and you did that in 4 days." I'll tell you, it's safe.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Russia/Ukraine/President Trump's Approach to Diplomacy

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Thank you, Mr. President. Last week you warned of what you called "severe consequences" if a 30-day cease-fire or any type of cease-fire were not agreed to by Russia. Will there be severe consequences? Does that change because of your meeting with President Putin?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. I don't think you need a cease-fire. You know, if you look at the six deals that I settled this year, they were all at war. I didn't do any cease-fires, and I know that it might be good to have. But I can also understand strategically, why, well, you know, one country or the other wouldn't want it. You have a cease-fire, and they rebuild and rebuild and rebuild, and you know, maybe they don't want that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But if you look at the six deals that we made peace on, you know, long-term, long-running wars—I didn't do any cease-fires. Would I like—I like the concept. You know, I like the concept of a cease-fire for one reason: because you'd stop killing people immediately, as opposed to in 2 weeks or 1 week or whatever it takes.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But we can work a deal where we're working on a peace deal while they're fighting. They have to fight. I wish they could stop. I'd like them to stop. But strategically, that could be a disadvantage for one side or the other. But all of these deals I made without even the mention of the words "cease-fire."

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/U.S. Security Assistance

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Can you explain the decision to offer Ukraine article 5–like security guarantees, but stop short of pushing for their full membership to NATO?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Yes. Well, we haven't done anything on that yet. If you look back and you go back long before President Putin, it was always a statement that they would never allow Ukraine into NATO. So that was a statement that was made.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But we haven't discussed any of that yet. We're going to be discussing it today. But we will give them very good protection, very good security.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. So——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. That's part of it. And the people that are waiting for us, they are—I think they're very likeminded. They want to—they want to help out also.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.] Peter.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Thank you. Thank you, President Trump.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Are you disappointed there's no cease-fire, Mr. President?

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Russia/Former President Joseph R. Biden, Jr.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. The United States has already given hundreds of billions of dollars to this war effort in Ukraine.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Biden.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. At best, it is a stalemate, and the killing continues. So, President Trump, how much more is the United States willing to give Ukraine? And, President Zelenskyy, how much more do you want?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, I'll start off just by saying we're not giving anything now. We're selling weapons. This is something before—I guess the number is well over $300 billion. That was under Joe Biden—a corrupt politician, not a smart man. Never was. By the way, go back 40 years. He was not a smart man 40 years ago, either. But now he's, in particular, bad.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: This was done by a corrupt administration that shouldn't have been in. And of the—and frankly, if the right results of the election were given, if I were President, this war would have never taken place. And he would have been very happy, because he would have liked to have seen—I mean, they went through hell. He went through hell.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: This war would have never happened. And the people that were killed, a couple of million people—a lot of people were soldiers and everything else—and the people that have been displaced and forced into other areas and other countries because of what's happened, none of that would have happened.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And I'm just saying that he was a horrible President. Whether it was the borders or this, he was just a horrible, corrupt President.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.] You want to answer the question?

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. Yes, I can. Thank you so much.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: So, first of all, we have possibility now to buy weapon from the United States. We are thankful for this program and this opportunity. We are thankful for Europe—they pay for this— and through NATO program for—[inaudible]—and et cetera. We have some programs where we can have some money to finance this. And this is a part, I think—it's not a part for the war and to defend us. It's also will be a part for security guarantees to strengthen our army, to rearm Ukrainian army.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: This is very, very important, and it depends how much money we need to rearm. For example, the question of air defense, we spoke about it with President Trump, and I am happy that we have now bilateral decisions, and we work on it with production—American production.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: Nobody in Europe has so many air defense, like Patriots, for example. We need it very much. And this is also about defending.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. And I think—you know, I think the good news—we make the best military equipment in the world, by far. You mentioned the Patriots. How good are they?

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. Yes, yes. Systems. Air defense.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. We have systems. They're literally 100-percent foolproof. And it's really like shooting two bullets—you know, two bullets hitting each other in the air, in a space like this. The chances—100 percent. It's 99 to 100 percent.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So we sell the equipment to NATO, and NATO does what—I don't know what the arrangement is that you have with—but I know that they want you to have the equipment. And we're getting the best equipment in the world, but they pay us for the equipment.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Under Biden, it was just crazy what was going on. I believe the number is over 300. I think it could be 350 billion dollars' worth of equipment and money and everything else.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And we've made more progress in settling this war in the last 2 months than they made in 4 years. This should have been settled a long time ago, but it should have never happened.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Yes, please.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Real quickly, you pushed out on social media——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Thank you, Mr. President. Was there—was there any miscommunication ——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Brian, go ahead—go first.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. President Zelenskyy, what security guarantees do you need from President Trump to be able to make a deal? Is it American troops? Intelligence? Equipment? What is it?

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. Everything. Really, we—it's includes two parts. First, strong Ukrainian army. Another one I began to discuss with your colleagues. And it's a lot about weapon and then people and training missions and intelligence. And second, it will—we will discuss with our partners. It depends on the big countries, on the United States, on a lot of our friends.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/U.S. Security Assistance

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. And, Mr. President, are you willing to commit American troops to that NATO-like protection in order to get President Zelenskyy to a deal today?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, I don't know if you define it that way, but NATO-like. I mean, we're going to give—we have people waiting in another room right now. They're all here, from Europe—biggest people in Europe. And they want to give protection. They feel very strongly about it, and we'll help them out with that. I think it's very important.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I think it's very important to get the deal done. [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Yes, please. Go ahead.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Ukraine/Russia

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President Trump, you have been involved to the peacekeeping in Ukraine since your first day in the administration. What would you say to the Ukrainian people right now, who are suffering under the Russian attacks and hoping that the American people will stand with them?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, I know Ukrainian people. I've known many over the years. They're great people. They're smart. They're energetic. They love their country. I mean, they love their country. And we want to get this war ended. That's all I can do. I love the Ukrainian people, but I love all people. I love the Russian people. I love them all. I want to get the war stopped. Very important.

context.speaker: Editorial
context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: President Trump's Diplomatic Efforts

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, was there any aspect of your discussion with Vladimir Putin that left you disappointed?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Look, we just spoke to—I was just telling the President—I just spoke to President Putin indirectly, and we're going to have a phone call right after these meetings today. And we may or may not have a trilat. If we don't have a trilat, then the fighting continues. And if we do, we have a good chance. I think if we have a trilat, there's a good chance of maybe ending it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But he's expecting my call when we're finished with this meeting. Thank you very much, everybody. Thank you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Thank you. Thank you, Peter.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: We had a good meeting, as you know, just a short while ago with the President of Russia. And I think there's a possibility that something could come out of it. And today's meeting is very important.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: We have, I guess, the seven—seven very powerful leaders from Europe, and we're going to be meeting with them right after this meeting. And thank you very much for being here.

favorable_source_context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
favorable_source_context.text: President Zelenskyy. Thank you so much, Mr. President. If I can, first of all——

favorable_source_context.speaker: Reporter
favorable_source_context.text: Q. And is this the end of the road for American support for Ukraine? Is today's meeting deal or no deal?

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: President Trump. I can never say that. It's never the end of the road. People are being killed, and we want to stop that. So I would not say it's the end of the road.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: No, I think we have a good chance of doing it. It's been almost 4 years now that—a lot of people were killed last week. A lot of people last week. I mean, millions of people killed, but a lot of people last week, for whatever reason. A big number. A lot of soldiers, both—on both sides.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: And I know the President, I know myself, and I believe Vladimir Putin wants to see it ended.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Reporter
favorable_source_context.text: Q. And as you—you met with Putin on Friday. Today you've got President Zelenskyy here. As you listen to Russia and Ukraine, which side has the better cards right now?

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: President Trump. Well, I don't want to say that. I'm just going to—I'm just here to be—look, this isn't my war. This is Joe Biden's war. He's the one that had a lot to do with this happening, and we want to get it ended. And we want it to end good for everybody. We want it to end good. The people of Ukraine have suffered incredibly. Incredibly.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Editorial
favorable_source_context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

favorable_source_context.speaker: Editorial_heading
favorable_source_context.text: Ukraine/Russia/President Trump's Foreign Policy

favorable_source_context.speaker: Reporter
favorable_source_context.text: Q. Mr. President, Vladimir Putin mentioned the—that the war will not end without addressing the root causes of this war. Do you—have you had an understanding what are the root causes of this war?

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: President Trump. Well, look, the war is going to end. When it ends, I can't tell you. But the war is going to end. And this gentleman wants it to end, and Vladimir Putin wants it to end. I think the whole world is tired of it. And we're going to get it ended.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: It was—you know, I've done six wars. I've ended six wars. And I thought this maybe would be the easiest one. [Laughter] And it's not the easiest one. It's a tough one. A lot of—a lot of reasons for it, and they'll be talking about it for a long time, but they'll be talking about the others.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: Look, India-Pakistan. We're talking about big places. When you look at—you just take a look at some of these wars. You—go to Africa and take a look at that: Rwanda and the Congo— Republic of the Congo. That's been going on for 31 years.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: President Trump. So the First Lady felt very strongly. She's watched the same thing that you watch and that I watch. I see things that you don't get to see, and it's horrible.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: But when—she's got a great love of children. She has a wonderful son that she loves probably more than anybody, including me, I hate to say it. But she loves her son. She loves children. And she hates to see—she hates to see something like this happening, and that goes for other wars too.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: I mean, she sees the—the heartbreak, the parents, the funerals that you see on television— always funerals. We want to see something other than funerals.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: No, she felt—it was a beautiful letter. He—it was very well received by him. And she did ask me to say—you know, she would love to see this end. She would love to see it end. And she says it very openly, very proudly, and with great sorrow, because so many people have been killed.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: Yes.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Editorial
favorable_source_context.text: [Several reporters spoke at once.]

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: No matter what I do, no matter what—and you know, this is not anything to do with you. It's probably to your advantage, in a certain way. But no matter what I do, no matter what deal I make, from my standpoint, you'll come out good, maybe President Putin will come out good, but they'll say, "Trump was absolutely horrible." It's just that—and I've lived with that for a long time. I've lived with it since just before the first election.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: I used to get great publicity. Now I get the worst publicity anyone's ever gotten in office. But I won in a landslide, so the people understand. They're the only ones that count, ultimately.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: But I've also had great reporters. I've had journalists that are very good.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: But it's very sad when you do the right thing—as an example, they said, "Because of the fact that Vladimir Putin came to American soil, this was a tremendous defeat for Donald Trump." No, it was really wonderful that he did it. It was a hard thing for him to do, to be honest with you. It was the opposite of what they said, but they said it.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: Now, if he didn't come, they'd say that was also bad for Trump. You know, there's no way. And there's just a great dishonesty of the press, and I think that's why it's lost its credibility. You know, its credibility is at an alltime low.

favorable_source_context.speaker: Trump
favorable_source_context.text: We have a thing going on right now in DC. We went from the most unsafe place anywhere to a place that now people—friends are calling me up, Democrats are calling me up, and they're saying: "Sir, I want to thank you. My wife and I went out to dinner last night for the first time in 4 years, and Washington, DC, is safe, and you did that in 4 days." I'll tell you, it's safe.

I think that's even overrated, largely overrated, but we're going to find out. And I think that the European nations are going to take a lot of the burden. We're going to help them, and we're going to make it very secure.

evidence.speaker: Trump
evidence.quote: We also need to discuss the possible exchanges of territory, taking into consideration the current line of contact—that means the war zone, the war lines that are pretty obvious—very sad, actually, to look at them—and negotiating positions.

evidence.speaker: Trump

evidence.speaker: Trump
evidence.quote: You know, in the six or so wars that we stopped, we haven't had a cease-fire, and so I don't know that it's necessary. But I believe a peace agreement at the end of all of this is something that's very attainable, and it can be done in the near future.

evidence.speaker: Trump
evidence.quote: And we'll see. In—at a—in a certain period of time, not very far from now—a week or 2 weeks—we're going to know whether or not we're going to solve this or is this horrible fighting going to continue. We'll do the best to get it ended.

evidence.speaker: Trump

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, thank you very much. It's a great honor to have you here. Special place. The White House is special, no matter where you're from. Represents so much, and it's— really is beautiful.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And thank you for all of the wonderful things that took place today. We've had a very successful day thus far and important discussions as we work to end the killing and stop the war in Ukraine. We're all working for the same goal. A very simple goal: We want to stop the killing, get this settled.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I've just had the honor of being with President Zelenskyy. In all of the discussions that we've had, we covered a lot of territory. And I spoke indirectly with President Putin today. We're going to call President Putin right after this meeting. I'm sure we're going to have a solid meeting, good meeting—maybe a great meeting. And we're going to try and work out a trilat after that and see if we can get it finished, put this to sleep, because this is—not since the Second World War has there been anything like this.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So I'm honored to welcome NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, who's a great gentleman; a great, great political leader in Europe, generally. But now he's the NATO Secretary General, and you're doing a fantastic job. Thank you very much, Mark.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Prime Minister Starmer of the United Kingdom, our friend and my friend and doing really well. And people like him a lot. We all like him.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: But you—we had a great negotiation, and you're respected all over the world. So, I want to thank you very much for being here. It's a great honor to have you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The Alaska summit reinforced my belief that, while difficult, peace is within reach, and I believe that. In a very significant step, President Putin agreed that Russia would accept security guarantees for Ukraine. And this is one of the key points that we need to consider, and we're going to be considering that at the table also—like who will do what, essentially.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I'm optimistic that, collectively, we can reach an agreement that would deter any future aggression against Ukraine. And I actually think there won't be. I think that's even overrated, largely overrated, but we're going to find out. And I think that the European nations are going to take a lot of the burden. We're going to help them, and we're going to make it very secure.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: We also need to discuss the possible exchanges of territory, taking into consideration the current line of contact—that means the war zone, the war lines that are pretty obvious—very sad, actually, to look at them—and negotiating positions.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Putin—also, you have President of Ukraine, who is—who you just met a little while ago, and we're going to try and get a three-party meeting, maybe, as soon as we can. And I have a feeling you and President Putin are going to work something out.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Ultimately, this is a decision that can only be made by President Zelenskyy and by the people of Ukraine working also together in agreement with President Putin. And I just think that's—very good things are going to come of it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So I hope we have a good meeting. And if we can have a good meeting, I'll set up a meeting with President Putin. And if you'd like, I'll go to that meeting, and not that I want to do that, but I will do that because we want to save a lot of people from dying. A lot of people are dying, and we got to save them. Got to save it. Five thousand, six thousand, seven thousand people, sometimes, a week.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: All of us would obviously prefer an immediate cease-fire while we work on a lasting peace, and maybe something like that could happen. As of this moment, it's not happening, but President Zelenskyy and President Putin can talk a little bit more about that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: You know, in the six or so wars that we stopped, we haven't had a cease-fire, and so I don't know that it's necessary. You can do it through the war, but it would be—I like the cease-fire from another standpoint: You immediately stop the killing. But I believe a peace agreement at the end of all of this is something that's very attainable, and it can be done in the near future.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: With all of the wars that I got involved in, we only have this one left. Of course, as I walk out the door, there'll probably be a new one starting, and I'll get that stopped too. But I thought

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I'd like to say—Mr. President, would you like to say something? You have the media. If you want, you could come over and you could stand—you could use mine, or you could just turn around, whichever you feel comfortable with.

context.speaker: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine
context.text: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine. Thank you so much. I can speak without microphone. Thank you so much.

context.speaker: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine
context.text: I think that we had very good conversation with President Trump.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Very good.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. And it really was the best one—or sorry, maybe the best one will be in the future, but it was really good. And we spoke about very sensitive points. The first one is security guarantees. And we are very happy with President that all the leaders are here, and the security in Ukraine depends on the United States and on you and on those leaders who are with us in our hearts. They have been online before yesterday and et cetera. So a lot of countries on the side of Ukraine, our people.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: And all of us want to finish this war, stop Russia, and stop this war. We spoke about it, and we will speak more about security guarantees. This is very important that United States gives such strong signal and is ready for security guarantees.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: The second point—or maybe the first—humanitarian direction, very important to exchange all the prisoners, and I think that President will help. And I was very thankful to your wife, again, Mr. President, for the letter about our abducted children. And I hope that, really, it can be historic role for the people to bring kids back to the families and be happy——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Get their people back, yes.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. ——in their families. Yes, this is so, so important, and I'm happy that we discussed it, this track with the President Trump. And I hope that we will find decisions.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: And then what is very important, that all the sensitive things—territorial and et cetera—we will discuss on the level of leaders during trilateral meeting, and President Trump will try to organize such meeting. And he said that he will come or not come. Ukraine will be happy if you will be able to participate.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. If you both want me there, I will be there. Yes. You know that.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. Yes, thank you. And I think this is very important. Yes.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: So security guarantees, bringing kids back, and all our people, not only warriors. First of all, warriors, and all the civilians, journalists—a lot of people in prison. So we need them back.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: And guarantees which will work for the years. We spoke about it, and I showed the President a lot of details on the battlefield, on the map. Thank you so much. Thank you for the map, by the way.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Good map.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. It was great, yes. [Laughter] I'm thinking how to take it back. [Laughter]

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. We'll get you one.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. No, no, no. I think that we had constructive, specific meeting. And I'm very thankful to all the leaders who are here, and you help a lot. And so we are happy that we have such big unity today.

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: Thank you, Mr. President——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Thank you very much——

context.speaker: President Zelenskyy
context.text: President Zelenskyy. ——for hosting us. Thank you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. ——Mr. President. And I think you'll see that President Putin really would like to do something else. I think when we set that up—when we do—I think it's going to be "when," not "if"—I think you're going to see some very, really positive moves.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: I know there's over a thousand prisoners, and I know they're going to release them. Maybe they're going to release them very soon—like, immediately—which I think is great. But we will—we're going to set that up today, after these—after this meeting.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: So, very good. And great remarks. I appreciate it.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Mark, as head of NATO, maybe you could say a few words, please.

context.speaker: Secretary General Mark Rutte of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization
context.text: Secretary General Mark Rutte of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Yes, I will be very brief. I really want to thank you, President of the United States, dear Donald, for the fact that you, as I said before, broke the deadlock, basically, with President Putin by starting that dialogue. And I think it was in February that you had first——
context.source_speaker_label: Secretary General Mark Rutte of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Right.

context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: Secretary General Rutte. ——phone call. And from there, we are now where we are today. And that is—I think if we play this well, we could end this. And we have to end it. We have to stop the killing. We have to stop the destruction of Ukraine's infrastructure. It is a terrible war.

context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: So I'm really excited. And let's make the best out of today and make sure that from today onwards, we get this thing to an end as soon as possible.

context.speaker: Secretary General Rutte
context.text: I really want to thank you for your leadership, what you are doing, Volodymyr, but, of course, also, all the European colleagues. It is really crucial.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. That's right.

context.speaker: President von der Leyen
context.text: President von der Leyen. ——agreed. And now we are here to work together with you on a just and lasting peace for Ukraine. Stop the killing. This is really our common interest: Stop the killing. And indeed, it's very good to hear that we're working on the security guarantees, article 5– like security guarantees. So important.

context.speaker: President von der Leyen
context.text: But I want to thank you also that you mentioned the thousands of Ukrainian children that have been abducted. And as a mother and grandmother, every single child has to go back to its family. This should be one of our main priorities also, in these negotiations, to make sure that the children come back to Ukraine to their families.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Thank you. And we did. I was just thinking—we're here for a different reason, but we just, a couple of weeks ago, made the largest trade deal in history. So, that's a big—that's a big thing. And congratulations. That's great.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: Thank you very much, Ursula.

context.speaker: Chancellor Merz
context.text: Chancellor Merz. You opened it last Friday. But now the way is open for complicated negotiations.

context.speaker: Chancellor Merz
context.text: And, to be honest, we all would like to see a cease-fire, the latest from the next meeting on. I can't imagine that the next meeting would took place without a cease-fire. So let's work on that, and let's try to put pressure on Russia, because the credibility of this efforts—these efforts we are undertaking today are depending on at least a cease-fire from the beginning of the serious negotiations, from next step on.

context.speaker: Chancellor Merz
context.text: So I would like to emphasize this aspect and would like to see a cease-fire from the next meeting, which should be a trilateral meeting, wherever it takes place.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, we're going to let the President go over and talk to the President. And we'll see how that works out. And if we can do that, I will say—and, again, I say it—in the six wars that I've settled, I haven't had a cease-fire. We just got into negotiations, and they—one of the wars was—as you know, in the Congo, was 30 years, 31 years long. Another one that we settled last week with two great countries was 35 years going on, and we had no cease-fire.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Meloni
context.text: Prime Minister Meloni. Well, thank you very much, Donald, Mr. President, for hosting us today in this important meeting. And I think it is an important day, a new phase, after 3 years and

context.speaker: Prime Minister Meloni
context.text: a half, that we didn't see any kind of sign from the Russian side that there was a willing for dialogue. So something is changing. Something has changed, thanks to you; thanks also to the stalling in the battlefield, which was achieved with the bravery of Ukrainians and with the unity that we all provided to Ukraine.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Meloni
context.text: And the reason why I mention it is that we also have to remind that if we want to reach peace and if we want to guarantee justice, we have to do it united. So that's why it's a very good day, the one we are in. You can obviously count on Italy. As it was from the beginning, we are on the side of Ukraine, and we do absolutely support your efforts towards peace.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Meloni
context.text: We will talk about many important topics. The first one is security guarantees, how to be sure that it won't happen again, which is the precondition of every kind of peace. I'm happy that we will discuss about that. I'm happy that we will begin from a proposal which is the, let's say, article 5 model, which was Italian at the beginning. So we are always ready to bring our proposals for peace, for dialogue. It's something we have to build together to guarantee peace and to defend the security of our Nation.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Meloni
context.text: So thank you——

context.speaker: President Emmanuel Macron of France
context.text: President Emmanuel Macron of France. Thank you, Mr. President, for organizing this meeting and for your commitment. And everything was said, but I have to—I just have to say here: Everybody around this table is in favor of peace. And we work very hard, and we've worked very hard during the past few years to have a peace which is a robust and longstanding peace.

context.speaker: President Emmanuel Macron of France
context.text: This is why the idea of a trilateral meeting is very important, because this is the only way to fix it. And by the way, I think in—as a follow-up, we would need probably a quadrilateral meeting because, when we speak about security guarantees, we speak about the whole security of the European continent. And this is why we are all united here with Ukraine on this matter.

context.speaker: President Emmanuel Macron of France
context.text: In order to organize such a trilateral meeting, your idea to ask for a truce or a cease-fire—at least to stop the killings, as we discussed—is a necessity. And we all support this idea.

context.speaker: President Emmanuel Macron of France
context.text: And in order to have such a longstanding peace for Ukraine and for the whole continent, we do need the security guarantees. And the first one is clearly a credible Ukrainian army for the years and decades to come. And the second one is our own commitment, all of us—and we worked very hard during the past few months amongst the "coalition of the willings," with the support of NATO—to build the different pillars of security guarantees and our commitments.

context.speaker: President Emmanuel Macron of France
context.text: And you can be sure that Europeans are very lucid about the fact that they have their fair share in the security guarantees for Ukraine, but their own security is clearly at stake in this situation.

context.speaker: President Emmanuel Macron of France
context.text: So you can count on us, as we can count on you, in order to deliver this robust peace for both Ukraine and Europe.

context.speaker: President Emmanuel Macron of France
context.text: Thank you.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Thank you very much, Emmanuel.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Keir Starmer of the United Kingdom
context.text: And thank you for hosting us here.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Keir Starmer of the United Kingdom
context.text: Can I start where Emmanuel started, which is we all want peace. The war in Ukraine has had a huge impact, particularly on the Ukrainians who have borne the brunt of it, but it's also had an impact on Europe and on the United Kingdom. There's not a family or community that hasn't been affected.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Keir Starmer of the United Kingdom
context.text: And when we talk about security, we're talking about the security not just of Ukraine. As a group, I think we've had a discussion on the phone a number of times, Mr. President, but be able now to be around the table to take it forward.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Keir Starmer of the United Kingdom
context.text: And I really feel that we can, I think, with the right approach this afternoon, make real progress, particularly on the security guarantees. context.speaker: Prime Minister Keir Starmer of the United Kingdom
context.text: With you coming alongside, the U.S. alongside what we've already developed, I think we can take a really important step forward today. A historic step, actually, could come out of this meeting in terms of security for Ukraine and security in Europe.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Keir Starmer of the United Kingdom
context.text: I also feel that we can make real progress towards a just and lasting outcome. Obviously, that has to involve Ukraine, and a trilateral meeting seems the sensible next step.

context.speaker: Prime Minister Keir Starmer of the United Kingdom
context.text: So thank you for being prepared to take that forward, because I think if we can ensure that that is the progress out of this meeting—both security guarantees and some sort of progress on trilateral meeting of some sort to bring some of the difficult issues to a head—then I think today will be seen as a very important day in recent years, in relation to a conflict which has gone on for three-and-a-bit years. And so far, nobody—nobody—has been able to bring it to this point. So, I thank you for that.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: President Trump. Well, thank you very much. And, you know, it's very interesting, because this is the first for the White House. You can't say that very often. context.text: Russia/Ukraine

context.text: The President. What would you like to know today?

context.text: Q. Could you start off by telling us the latest one with Russia and Ukraine? Are you expecting——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Well, we're having——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Are you expecting Zelenskyy to come visit you?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. We're having good—I don't know. He would like to come, but I think we should get a deal done first. We're having good talks. We started with Russia. context.speaker: Trump
context.text: And we won't know for a little while, but we'll—we're making progress.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. You said—what other things did you——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. We settled eight wars, and I thought this would be one of the easier ones because of my relationship with President Putin, but this is probably one of the more difficult ones. There's a lot of hatred.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: U.S. Diplomatic Efforts/Ukraine/Russia

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Mr. President, you said that there were a few points of disagreement that were still left to be——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Yes, a few. A few.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Can you tell us what those are, what the points of disagreement are?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Well, it's the—standard things, but people are starting to realize it's a good deal for both parties. They got to stop the war. They're losing a lot of people—a lot of soldiers. Mostly soldiers.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. In that 28-point plan——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Yes.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. ——that was originally leaked, there were some portions of that that said that Ukraine needed to cut——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Well, that was an original proposal. And then, from there, we went back and forth.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Negotiations in the Ukraine-Russia Conflict

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. So, when it comes to ceding land to Russia, is that still on the table, or has that changed?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Well, they're talking about going land both ways and trying to clean up a border. You know, you can't go through the middle of a house, you can't go through the middle of a highway. So they're trying to work something. It's a complicated process. It doesn't go that quickly.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Do you think Russia——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. The U.S.——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. What about security—what about security guarantees and Ukraine joining NATO?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Well, we're working that out with Europe. Europe will be largely involved in that. We're working that out with Europe. Europe really wants to see it end, if possible.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. There were a lot of Republicans who felt that the first plan, the first 28-point plan, was too favorable to Russia. Have you changed that?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Well, that was just a map. All that was is a map. That was not a plan. It was a concept. And from there, they've taken each one of the 28 points, and then you got down to 22 points. A lot of them were solved and, actually, very favorably solved. So we'll see how—we'll see what happens.

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Do you think——

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Does the same——

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Russia/Ukraine/U.S. Diplomatic Efforts

context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Do you think that Russia—that Ukraine was being asked to give too much land back to Russia? I know at one point you said they——

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Well——

context.speaker: Q. ——
context.text: Q. ——shouldn't have to give any back.

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. Yes. It's really up—look, the way it's going, if you look, it's just moving in one direction. context.speaker: Trump
context.text: In some cases, the land is going in the other direction. So they're negotiating. They're trying to get it done. So it's a long, complicated process and very—very sad because so many people are being killed.

context.text: Q. What's the next step?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. They're going to keep talking. They're talking to Russia now. Steve Witkoff is going over, maybe with Jared. context.speaker: Reporter
context.text: Q. Next week in Moscow?

context.speaker: Trump
context.text: The President. I think so, yes.

context.speaker: Editorial_heading
context.text: Negotiations in Ukraine-Russia Conflict
